8.s: What does social change mean, in sociology?
o: Alteration in the social order (structure and relationships)

8.s: Which technological change of 1760-1820 was the term popularised in English by Arnold Toynbee?
8.x: Technology – Industrial Revolution (Watt, Hargreaves; term popularised in English by Arnold Toynbee, 1760-1820); internet – 820 million+ users (Dec 2025)

8.s: Which 1955 law is an example of law as a source of social change in India?

8.x: Media – Spreads awareness, forms opinion; cultural diffusion; behaviour-change communication (ES 2025-26)

8.s: Which concept of Merton does a literacy drive that also raises health awareness illustrate?

8.s: Who wrote The Decline of the West, a cyclical theory of social change?

8.s: Which scholars are proponents of the diffusion theory of social change?

8.s: Who wrote The Theory of the Leisure Class, a technological theory of change?
8.x: Technological – Veblen (*Theory of the Leisure Class*), Ogburn (adaptive culture, cultural lag)

8.s: Which thinker is linked with the biological theory of struggle and "survival of the fittest"?
8.x: Biological / evolutionary struggle – Darwin – survival of the fittest ("worthy living")

8.s: Whose idea came after Spencer's in the chronology of evolutionary theory?
8.x: Chronology – Comte's positivism → Spencer → Durkheim's division of labour

8.s: Which Social Darwinist wrote Folkways (1906) on in-group/out-group antagonism?
8.x: W.G. Sumner (*Folkways*, 1906) – Social Darwinist; in-group/out-group antagonism and struggle – usually grouped with the early conflict school

8.s: What three stages of socio-cultural evolution did L.H. Morgan describe in Ancient Society (1877)?
8.x: L.H. Morgan (*Ancient Society*, 1877) – Three stages of socio-cultural evolution – savagery (wild), barbarism, civilisation

8.s: Which British diffusionists traced culture to Egypt as its source?

8.x: British – Elliot Smith, Perry – Egypt as the source

8.s: Which German-Austrian scholars developed the "culture circles" school of diffusion?

8.s: What concept is linked with the German-Austrian diffusionists Graebner and Schmidt?

8.s: Which American scholars developed the "culture areas" concept of diffusion?

8.s: What concept is linked with the American diffusionists Boas and Wissler?
8.x: American – Boas, Wissler – Culture areas

8.s: What is the process in which a group, through sustained contact, is influenced by a dominant culture but stays distinct?
8.x: Acculturation – Change through sustained contact: a group is influenced by another (dominant) culture and its way of life changes, but it stays distinct

8.s: What is the process in which immigrants lose their own cultural identity and are absorbed into the host culture?
8.x: Assimilation ("merger") – A group (e.g. immigrants) loses its own cultural identity and is absorbed into the host/dominant culture

8.s: What is the term for taking part in the wider society while retaining one's own identity?
8.x: Integration – Taking part in the wider society while retaining identity

8.s: Which process of culture contact is described as the "melting pot", a fusion of groups into a new one?
8.x: Amalgamation – Biological/cultural fusion of groups into a new one ("melting pot")

8.s: What is the peaceful coexistence of distinct groups and cultures in one society called?
8.x: Cultural pluralism / multiculturalism – Peaceful coexistence of distinct groups and cultures in one society

8.x: Cultural diffusion – Spread of culture (e.g. through media)

8.s: What is understanding a culture on its own terms called?

8.s: What is xenocentrism?
o: Understanding a culture on its own terms
Seeing one's own group as superior
Preferring other cultures to one's own
8.x: Xenocentrism / Xenophobia – Preferring other cultures / fear of foreigners

8.s: In which process of culture contact is a group's own identity lost?
8.x: Pluralism = coexistence; amalgamation = fusion; assimilation = identity lost; acculturation = influenced but distinct.

8.s: Who wrote The Aborigines So-Called and Their Future, arguing for tribal assimilation?
8.x: Ghurye, *The Aborigines So-Called and Their Future*: argued for tribal assimilation (tribes as "backward Hindus").

8.s: In which book did M.N. Srinivas first use the term Sanskritisation (1952)?

8.s: Whose customs and rituals does a low caste or tribe adopt under Sanskritisation?

8.x: *The Remembered Village*; *Village, Caste, Gender and Method* – M.N. Srinivas

8.x: *Caste and Race in India* – G.S. Ghurye

55.s: Who described India as "federal in form, unitary in spirit"?

55.s: Which country's states, unlike Indian States, have separate constitutions and dual citizenship?
55.x: Indian States vs the USA – Indian States have no separate constitutions and no dual citizenship; the USA has both

55.s: What is a State that upholds no religion as the official religion called?
55.x: Secular state – It does not uphold any religion as the official religion – the Indian State has no religious basis

55.s: By which Amendment does the Preamble describe India as a secular State?
55.x: "Secular" added to the Preamble – By the 42nd Amendment, 1976 → the Preamble describes India as a secular State

55.s: What is the positive (Indian) model of secularism?
o: Complete separation of State and religion
55.x: Indian model (positive) – Equal respect to / equal protection of all religions

55.s: What is the negative (Western) model of secularism?
o: Complete separation of State and religion
55.x: Western model (negative) – Complete separation of State and religion

55.s: Which Articles of the Constitution guarantee freedom of religion?
55.x: Secular provisions – Preamble; Arts. 14, 15, 16, 25-28 (freedom of religion), 29, 30, 44

55.s: What is the status of a theocratic (religious) State under the Indian Constitution?
o: Not a feature of the Constitution
55.x: Religious (theocratic) state – Not a feature of the Constitution

55.s: Which DPSP Article on organising agriculture and animal husbandry covers cow protection?

56.s: What kind of government is a constitutional government by definition?
56.x: Constitutional government – By definition = limited government – a government limited by the terms of the Constitution

56.s: Which principle does "Persons may change but rules should not change" express?
56.x: "Persons may change but rules should not change" – Principle of constitutional government (rule of law, not of persons)

56.s: What limits the powers of government in a democracy?
56.x: Powers of government in a democracy – Limited by the Constitution

56.s: What is the idea that a legislative majority cannot override constitutional limits called?
56.x: Constitutionalism – Limits + rule of law + checks and balances + judicial review + FRs; a legislative majority cannot override constitutional limitations

56.s: What does true democracy mean more than, besides free elections and equality before law?
56.x: Marks of true democracy – Free and fair elections, respect for the individual, equality before law – more than "rule by majority only"

56.s: What is the place of Public Interest Litigation in the rule of law in India?
56.x: PIL – Not indispensable for the rule of law, which existed before PIL through Arts. 14, 32, 226

56.s: Which thinker, in Leviathan (1651), argued for the absolute sovereign power of the monarch?
56.x: Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) – Absolute sovereign power of the monarch

56.s: Which thinker argued for limited government and the natural rights of life, liberty and property?
56.x: John Locke – Limited government, natural rights (life, liberty, property)

56.s: Who wrote The Social Contract (1762) on the general will and popular sovereignty?
56.x: J.-J. Rousseau – The Social Contract (1762); general will, popular sovereignty

56.s: Who held, in Natural Rights (1895), that rights grow out of custom?
56.x: D.G. Ritchie (*Natural Rights*, 1895) – Customary (historical) rights – rights grow out of custom

56.s: Which school of thought calls the State a necessary evil to be kept minimal?
56.x: Individualists – State a necessary evil – keep it minimal

56.s: Which school calls the State an unnecessary evil to be abolished?
56.x: Anarchists – State an unnecessary evil – abolish it

56.s: In which year did Montesquieu publish "The Spirit of Laws"?
56.x: Montesquieu – Division of powers best protects liberty; "The Spirit of Laws" (1748); drew on the British constitution

56.s: What is considered the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy?
56.x: Best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy – Separation of powers

56.s: On which principle does presidential government operate?
56.x: Presidential government – Operates on separation of powers

56.s: What marks the parliamentary system's relation between ministers and the legislature?
56.x: Parliamentary government – Fusion – ministers drawn from and responsible to the legislature

56.s: What is the division of powers between the Centre and States called?
56.x: Division of powers between Centre and States – Federalism

56.s: Which organ of government consists of the people's elected representatives?
56.x: Organ of the people's elected representatives – The legislature (judges are appointed; the media is not an organ of government)

56.s: Who is the real executive in India?
56.x: Heads – Nominal head President; real executive Council of Ministers

56.s: What did Ambedkar prefer over stability in choosing the parliamentary system?
56.x: Ambedkar – Preferred responsibility over stability; reasons: familiarity (1919/1935 Acts), diversity, avoiding American-style deadlock

56.s: In which 1955 case did the Supreme Court say India has no rigid separation of powers?
56.x: Nature in India – No rigid separation – implicit, not absolute, functional; overlaps → checks and balances (Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955)

56.s: In which case was separation of powers held to be a basic feature of the Constitution?
56.x: Basic feature – Separation of powers (Kesavananda, 1973)

56.s: Which DPSP Article asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive?
56.x: Art. 50 (DPSP) – Separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State

56.s: Which Article bars Parliament from discussing a judge's conduct except in removal proceedings?
56.x: Judiciary insulated – Arts. 50, 121, 211, 235

56.s: Which official got back magisterial and police powers under Munro's Madras Regulations of 1816?
56.x: Munro's Madras Regulations (1816) – Reversed the Cornwallis separation – the Collector again got magisterial and police powers

56.s: To whom is the executive subordinate in India's parliamentary system?
56.x: In India the executive is subordinate to the legislature – the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

56.s: What is the main purpose of Question Hour and Zero Hour in Parliament?
56.x: Question Hour, Zero Hour – Daily watch

56.s: In which House can a no-confidence motion to remove the government be moved?
56.x: No-confidence motion – Removes the government – Lok Sabha only

56.s: Who is removed by impeachment under Article 61?
56.x: Impeachment (Art. 61) – Removes the President

56.s: Which Article makes the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha?
56.x: Collective responsibility – Art. 75(3) Lok Sabha; 164(2) Assembly

56.s: Which Article lets the President summon and prorogue Parliament, with at most a six-month gap?
56.x: Summon/prorogue; max 6-month gap – Art. 85 – Art. 174

56.s: Which Article lets the Governor summon and prorogue the State legislature?
56.x: Summon/prorogue; max 6-month gap – Art. 85 – Art. 174

56.s: Which Article empowers the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha?
56.x: Dissolve lower House – Art. 85(2) – Assembly (174(2))

56.s: Which Article empowers the Governor to dissolve the State Assembly?
56.x: Dissolve lower House – Art. 85(2) – Assembly (174(2))

56.s: Which Articles cover the President's address and messages to Parliament?
56.x: Address / messages – 86, 87 – 175, 176

56.s: Which Articles cover the Governor's address and messages to the State legislature?
56.x: Address / messages – 86, 87 – 175, 176

56.s: Which Article empowers the Governor to promulgate ordinances?
56.x: Ordinance – 123 – 213

56.s: Which power: 111?
56.x: Assent / veto – 111 – 200; reserve 201

56.s: When can an ordinance be issued?
o: Only when the legislature is not in session
56.x: Ordinance only when the legislature is not in session; subject to judicial review; laid before the House.

56.s: What power do Articles 13, 32 and 226 give the courts?
o: Judicial review of laws and executive action
56.x: Arts. 13, 32, 226 – Judicial review of laws and executive action; an ultra vires law is void

56.s: Which article: No discussion in Parliament (State legislature) on an SC/HC judge's conduct except on a removal motion?
56.x: Art. 121 / Art. 211 – No discussion in Parliament (State legislature) on an SC/HC judge's conduct except on a removal motion

56.s: What do Articles 122 and 212 bar the courts from doing?
o: Questioning legislative proceedings for irregular procedure
56.x: Arts. 122, 212 – Courts cannot question legislative proceedings for irregular procedure

56.s: Under which Article did the Supreme Court issue the Vishaka guidelines to do "complete justice"?
56.x: Art. 142 – Complete justice – fills gaps (Vishaka before the POSH Act, 2013)

56.s: Which case of 1955 held that India has no rigid separation of powers?
56.x: Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) – No rigid separation

56.s: In which case was separation of powers held a basic feature of the Constitution?
56.x: Kesavananda (1973) – Separation of powers = basic feature

56.s: Which Amendment's validation of the PM's election was struck down in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)?
56.x: Raj Narain (1975) – Legislature cannot decide an election dispute; 39th Amendment validation of PM's election struck down

56.s: Which Amendment's bar on judicial review was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)?
56.x: Minerva Mills (1980) – 42nd Amendment bar on review struck down

56.s: After which date are laws put in the Ninth Schedule open to review, per I.R. Coelho (2007)?
56.x: I.R. Coelho (2007) – Post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule entries reviewable

56.s: What limits Parliament when it overrides a judgment by constitutional amendment?
56.x: Constitutional amendment – Basic structure

56.s: What must a validating law do to override a court judgment?
o: Remove the basis of the judgment
56.x: Validating law – Must remove the basis; cannot simply declare the judgment void

56.s: Which case made Ninth Schedule laws, such as Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation, open to review?
56.x: Ninth Schedule (76th, TN 69%) – Coelho review

56.s: What is the status of the Supreme Court's advice to the President under Article 143?
56.x: Review Art. 137; reference Art. 143 – Art. 143 advice not binding

56.s: Which Amendment overrode the Golaknath judgment?
56.x: 1st / 24th / 26th / 77th Amendment – Overrode Champakam / Golaknath / Madhav Rao (privy purses) / Indra Sawhney

56.s: How does Parliament override a court judgment?
o: By changing the law or its constitutional basis
56.x: Parliament overrides a judgment by changing the law or constitutional basis – not by a simple resolution.

56.s: In which year was the One Nation One Election Bill (129th Amendment Bill) introduced?
56.x: One Nation One Election Bill (129th Amendment Bill, 2024): amends Arts. 83, 172, 327 (and adds 82A).

57.s: Which commission's report was one of the bases of the Government of India Act, 1935?
57.x: Based on – The Simon Commission report, the Round Table Conferences (the third RTC) and the White Paper (1933)

57.s: How many sections and schedules did the Government of India Act, 1935 have?
57.x: Size – 321 sections, 10 schedules (14 parts) – the longest Act passed by the British Parliament up to then

57.s: Who called the Government of India Act, 1935 "a machine with strong brakes but no engine"?
57.x: Nehru's verdict – A "Charter of Slavery" / "a machine with strong brakes but no engine"

57.s: Which Act first provided for a federal polity, an "All-India Federation", in India?
57.x: All-India Federation – British provinces + princely states – the first provision for a federal polity in India; the Act's own name = "Federation of India" (Part II, s.5)

57.s: Why did the All-India Federation of the 1935 Act never come into being?
o: The princely states did not join
57.x: Never came into being – Joining was optional for the princes and the rulers of princely states did not consent to join

57.s: What was the real British aim behind the All-India Federation of 1935?
o: To use the princes to counter-balance the nationalists
57.x: Real British intention – To use the princes to counter-balance the nationalist leaders

57.s: How many items did the Federal List of the 1935 Act have?
57.x: Three lists – Federal (59 items), Provincial (54), Concurrent (36) – first division of legislative powers between Centre and provinces; basis of today's Centre–State scheme

57.s: With whom were the residuary powers vested under the 1935 Act?
57.x: Residuary powers – The Governor-General (not the federal or provincial legislature, not the Governors)

57.s: Which subjects were to be "reserved" under the proposed dyarchy at the Centre in 1935?
57.x: Dyarchy at the Centre – Proposed: defence and foreign affairs = reserved subjects under the Governor-General – never implemented

57.s: Which two Houses did the 1935 Act propose for the federal legislature?
o: Legislative Assembly and Council of State
House of the People and Senate
Federal Assembly and Council of States
57.x: Bicameral Centre (proposed) – Federal Assembly + Council of States

57.s: When did responsible ministries start in the provinces under the 1935 Act?
57.x: Provincial autonomy – The most important feature; it abolished provincial dyarchy (of 1919); responsible ministries from April 1937

57.s: Which province did NOT have a bicameral legislature under the 1935 Act?
57.x: Bicameral legislatures in 6 of 11 provinces – Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam, United Provinces (Punjab was unicameral)

57.s: Which special power did Governors keep under the 1935 Act?
57.x: Governors – Kept special powers: veto, ordinances and power to legislate on their own (Governor's Acts)

57.s: To which groups did the 1935 Act extend communal representation?
57.x: Communal representation – Extended to depressed classes, women and labour

57.s: Which territory was separated from India under the 1935 Act?
57.x: New provinces – Burma separated from India; Sindh carved from Bombay, Orissa from Bihar

57.s: What share of the population got the vote under the 1935 Act?
57.x: Franchise – About 14% of the population (about 3.5 crore voters); still no adult franchise

57.s: In which province did the Unionist Party, not the Congress, form the ministry after the 1937 elections?
57.x: 1937 elections – Congress formed ministries in most provinces, but not in Punjab (Unionist Party) or Bengal

57.s: What did the 1935 Act do to provincial dyarchy?
57.x: The 1935 Act ended provincial dyarchy and only proposed central dyarchy – it brought no dyarchy at both levels.

57.s: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Federal Court inaugurated in 1937?
57.x: Federal Court (Delhi) – Inaugurated 1 October 1937; first CJ Sir Maurice Gwyer; replaced by the Supreme Court in 1950

57.s: When was the Reserve Bank of India set up?
57.x: RBI – Set up on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934

57.s: Which Public Service Commissions did the 1935 Act provide for?
57.x: Public Service Commissions – Federal, Provincial and Joint PSCs (no "All-India Services Commission")

57.s: What did the 1935 Act do to the Council of India?
57.x: Council of India – Abolished; the Secretary of State got a team of advisers instead

57.s: About how many provisions of the Constitution came from the GoI Act 1935?
57.x: Main source of the Constitution – About 250 provisions / "nearly 75%" – federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary, PSCs, emergency provisions, administrative details

57.s: Which power of the President under Article 123 is a relic of Section 42 of the 1935 Act?
57.x: Section 42 → Article 123 – President's ordinance power – a relic of the 1935 Act

57.s: Which Article on the Governor's address derives from Section 63 of the 1935 Act?
57.x: Section 63 → Article 175 – Governor's address

57.s: To which source is the pattern of Centre-State relations in the Constitution traced?
57.x: Centre–State relations pattern – Traced to the 1935 Act (not the US Constitution or the Nehru Report)

57.s: What did the 1935 Act do to communal representation?
57.x: The 1935 Act abolished dyarchy in the Governors' provinces and kept the Governors' power to veto and legislate; it extended communal representation.

57.s: Which act: Monopoly extended 20 years; override power extended to all later GGs and Presidency Governors; more control over…?
57.x: 1793 – Monopoly extended 20 years; override power extended to all later GGs and Presidency Governors; more control over Bombay and Madras; Board of Control salaries charged to Indian revenues; C-in-C not a council member

57.s: Which act: Trade monopoly in India ended except tea and China trade; Christian missionaries allowed; Rs 1 lakh a year for…?
57.x: 1813 – Trade monopoly in India ended except tea and China trade; Christian missionaries allowed; Rs 1 lakh a year for education (first such provision); first asserted Crown sovereignty over Company territories

57.s: Which Section of the Charter Act 1833 said no Indian would be debarred from office by religion, birth or colour?
57.x: 1833 (Saint Helena Act) – GG of Bengal → Governor-General of India (William Bentinck – last GG of Bengal, first GG of India); Company's commercial functions ended – purely administrative; Law Member added (council to 4) – Macaulay; Law Commission under Macaulay; legislation centralised; Section 87: no Indian debarred by religion, birth, descent or colour; GG-in-Council to mitigate and abolish slavery

57.s: Which Charter Act created the Indian Legislative Council called a "mini-parliament"?
57.x: 1853 (last Charter Act) – Legislative and executive functions separated; 6 legislative members added – Indian (Central) Legislative Council, the first legislature / "mini-parliament"; open competition for civil services (Macaulay Committee 1854); territories held "in trust for Her Majesty", no fixed term

57.s: Which trade did the Company keep after the Charter Act of 1813 ended its Indian monopoly?
57.x: Trade – Ended the trade monopoly in India – but kept tea and China trade

57.s: Which Charter Act permitted Christian missionary activity in India?
57.x: Missionaries – Christian missionary activity permitted (Charles Grant, Wilberforce)

57.s: Which Charter Act granted Rs 1 lakh a year for education in India?

57.s: Who became the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833?
57.x: Designation – Governor-General of Bengal designated Governor-General of India – first GG of India Bentinck (1833)

57.s: What did the Governor-General-in-Council get for the whole of British India under the Charter Act of 1833?
57.x: Centralisation – Final step towards centralisation; GG-in-Council got all law-making powers for the whole of British India – often called the beginning of constitution-making under British rule

57.s: Who was the first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council under the 1833 Act?

57.s: In which year was slavery abolished in India by Act V?
57.x: Slavery – Government to take measures to abolish slavery and improve the condition of slaves (→ Slavery Act V of 1843)

57.s: When was the Indian Penal Code enacted?
57.x: IPC dates – Drafted by Macaulay's First Law Commission (1837); enacted 6 Oct 1860; came into force 1 Jan 1862

57.s: Which body is regarded as the first official legislature in India?
57.x: First official legislature – The separate Legislative Council of 1853

57.s: From which year was the civil services examination held after the 1853 Act opened it to competition?
57.x: Civil services – Appointments by patronage of the Directors till 1853; the 1853 Act threw them open to competition (exam from 1855)

57.s: Which Act was the first in the line Pitt's India Act, Charter Acts and Indian Councils Act 1861?
57.x: Order of Acts – Regulating Act 1773 → Pitt's India Act 1784 → Charter Acts (1793 onwards) → Indian Councils Act 1861

57.s: What gradual goal did Montagu's declaration of 20 August 1917 announce?
57.x: Montagu's declaration, 20 August 1917 – "Increasing association of Indians in every branch of administration" and gradual responsible government

57.s: In which year was the Montagu-Chelmsford Report published?
57.x: Report – Montagu-Chelmsford Report 1918

57.s: Who was the Viceroy during the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms?
57.x: Persons – Edwin Montagu = Secretary of State; Lord Chelmsford = Viceroy

57.s: Into which two groups were provincial subjects divided under the 1919 dyarchy?

57.s: Who administered the reserved subjects under the 1919 dyarchy?
o: The Governor with his Executive Council
57.x: Reserved subjects – Administered by the Governor with his Executive Council (not answerable to the legislature)

57.s: Who administered the transferred subjects under the 1919 dyarchy?
o: The Governor with Indian ministers responsible to the legislature
57.x: Transferred subjects – Governor with Indian ministers responsible to the legislative council

57.s: Which Act separated central and provincial budgets for the first time?
57.x: Central and provincial subjects separated – It clearly defined the jurisdiction of the central and provincial governments; budgets separated for the first time

57.s: How many members did the Legislative Assembly under the 1919 Act have?
57.x: Bicameral central legislature – First time: Council of State (upper, 60) + Legislative Assembly (lower, 145: 104 elected + 41 nominated); direct elections on a limited franchise (property, tax, education)

57.s: How many of the six members of the Viceroy's Executive Council were to be Indians under the 1919 Act?
57.x: Responsible government – Term "responsible government" first used; 3 of the 6 members of the Viceroy's Executive Council to be Indians

57.s: To which groups did the 1919 Act extend communal representation?
57.x: Communal representation extended – To Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans

57.s: When was the Public Service Commission set up under the 1919 Act?
57.x: New offices – High Commissioner for India in London; Public Service Commission – set up 1 October 1926 (Chairman + 4); Public Accounts Committee 1921

57.s: By which year had Indians outnumbered Europeans in the ICS?
57.x: Civil services – ICS examination held in India too (from 1922); by 1941 Indians outnumbered Europeans in the ICS

57.s: How many members did the Chamber of Princes set up in 1921 have?
57.x: Chamber of Princes – 120 members; King George V's Proclamation, 23 December 1919; first Chancellor Ganga Singh of Bikaner

57.s: In which year was the Simon Commission appointed?
57.x: Statutory commission after 10 years – Simon Commission appointed 1927 (two years early) – 7 British members under Sir John Simon; "Simon Go Back"

57.s: When were the first elections under the 1919 Act held?
57.x: First elections – November 1920 (boycotted by the Congress during Non-Cooperation); the new legislatures met in 1921

57.s: In which year was the last election to the central legislature under the 1919 Act held?
57.x: Last election of the central legislature under this Act – 1945

57.s: Which of these was a transferred subject under the 1919 dyarchy?
57.x: Police, administration of justice, land revenue, law and order, irrigation, finance – Local self-government, education, public health, agriculture, public works

57.s: After which event was rule over British India transferred from the Company to the Crown?
57.x: Rule transferred from the East India Company to the British Crown – Main administrative consequence of the Revolt of 1857; British India under direct Crown rule from 1858

57.s: Which Act was titled 'An Act for the Good Government of India'?
57.x: Name and purpose – "Act for the Good Government of India" – for a more responsible management of Indian affairs after the revolt exposed Company misrule

57.s: Who was the first Governor-General to be styled Viceroy?
57.x: Governor-General also styled Viceroy – Lord Canning first; last Viceroy Mountbatten

57.s: What ended with the abolition of the Board of Control and the Court of Directors in 1858?
57.x: Board of Control and Court of Directors abolished – Dual government ended

57.s: Which new office under the 1858 Act issued instructions to the Governor-General?
o: President of the Board of Control
57.x: Secretary of State for India – Created – a member of the British cabinet with a 15-member Council of India; he issued instructions to the Governor-General; the Crown's powers were exercised through him

57.s: What is Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1 November 1858 called?
57.x: Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858) – Called the "Magna Carta of Indian liberties"

57.s: How much did the Act of 1767 require the Company to pay the British Government each year?
57.x: Act of 1767 – The Company to pay the British Government £400,000 a year

57.s: Whose committee report led Parliament to pass the Regulating Act after the 1772 crisis?

57.s: Who headed Fort William between 1757 and 1772?

57.s: Which was the first step by the British Parliament to control the East India Company?

57.s: Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773?

57.s: Which Presidencies were made subordinate to Bengal by the Regulating Act of 1773?

57.s: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta set up in 1774?

57.s: What did the Regulating Act of 1773 ban for Company servants?

57.s: Which Act required the Directors to send letters on revenue, civil and military affairs to the British Government?
57.x: Correspondence – Directors to send letters on revenue, civil and military affairs to the British Government

57.s: When was the Court of Directors, kept by the Regulating Act, finally abolished?

57.s: What did the Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) do?
57.x: Amending Act 1781 (Act of Settlement) – Separated judicial and executive functions

57.s: How many members did the Board of Control under Pitt's India Act have?
57.x: Dual control / double government – Board of Control (political, 6 members) + Court of Directors (commercial)

57.s: What were the Company's territories called under Pitt's India Act, 1784?

57.s: Who first used the power under the Act of 1786 to override his council?

57.s: In which year did power pass from the Company to the Crown?

57.s: Which Presidencies got back their legislative powers under the Indian Councils Act, 1861?

57.s: Who criticised the absence of Indians in the council as a lesson of 1857?

57.s: In which year did Canning begin the portfolio system?

57.s: How long at most was an ordinance by the Viceroy valid under the 1861 Act?

57.s: Which High Courts were set up in 1862 under the Indian High Courts Act 1861?
57.x: Indian High Courts Act 1861 – High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1862)

57.s: Which bodies could recommend members for nomination under the 1892 Act's indirect election?

57.s: What could members do with the budget under the Indian Councils Act, 1892?

57.s: How many days' notice was needed to ask a question under the Indian Councils Act, 1892?

57.s: In what capacity were Indians associated with the councils under the 1861 Act?
57.x: Indians – Nominated non-officials – More non-officials

57.s: What change did the 1892 Act make to non-official members of the councils?
57.x: Indians – Nominated non-officials – More non-officials

57.s: Which Act first introduced indirect election to the legislative councils?
57.x: Election – None – Indirect begins

57.s: What could the councils do with the budget under the 1861 Act?

57.s: Which two features got statutory recognition under the Indian Councils Act, 1861?

57.s: Which new right did the 1892 Act give council members?

64.x: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

64.s: In what order does the Preamble describe India?
64.x: Order of the description – Sovereign → Socialist → Secular → Democratic → Republic

64.s: In what order does the Preamble list its objectives?
64.x: Order of objectives – Justice → Liberty → Equality → Fraternity

64.s: Which part of the Constitution declares India secular?
64.x: India is declared secular by the Preamble – Fundamental Rights, DPSP and the 9th Schedule do not "describe" India as secular

64.s: How does the Preamble describe India now?
64.x: Description of India – "Sovereign Democratic Republic" – "Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic"

64.s: Which of these words is absent from the Preamble?
64.x: Description – Federal / federation; "Quasi-federal"; "Reliable", "Non-religious"

64.s: Which word does the Preamble not use, using "Liberty" instead?
64.x: Other terms – Freedom (it uses Liberty), Right (as a word), Public Welfare / Welfare State, Adult franchise, Fundamental Duties, "People's"

64.s: Which kind of justice is not mentioned in the Preamble?
64.x: Justice – Religious Justice, Natural or Cultural justice – justice is only social, economic, political

64.s: Which of these is NOT a liberty named in the Preamble?
64.x: Liberty – Political Liberty and Economic Liberty as categories; liberty "of action" – liberty is only of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship

64.s: Of what does the Preamble promise equality?
64.x: Equality – Of nationality, religion or community – equality is of status and opportunity

64.s: Which of these words appears in the Preamble?
64.x: Words that are in it: Fraternity, Equality, Justice, Unity, Integrity, Thought, Opportunity, Dignity, Republic, Sovereign.

64.s: Which Preamble term means supreme authority, free internally and externally?
64.x: Sovereign – Supreme authority; free internally and externally; not subject to any external authority

64.s: What kind of economy does "Socialist" in the Preamble imply?
64.x: Socialist – Democratic socialism – a mixed economy (public and private sectors); a blend of Marxism and Gandhism, leaning towards Gandhian socialism

64.s: In which provision did the word "secular" appear before 1976?
64.x: Secular – Equal respect for all religions; no State religion; before 1976 the word appeared only in Art. 25(2)(a); the term is not defined in any Article

64.s: Which kinds of democracy does "Democratic" in the Preamble cover?
64.x: Democratic – Government by the people; representative parliamentary democracy; covers political, social and economic democracy; universal adult franchise and rule of law are its marks

64.s: What is absent in a republic, besides the head of State being elected?
64.x: Republic – Elected head of State (the President, indirectly elected for 5 years); no hereditary element; public offices open to all

64.s: Why is India a republic?
o: Its head of State is elected
64.x: Republic ≠ PM: India is a republic because its head of State (President) is elected – not because ministers are responsible to Parliament or hold office at the President's pleasure.

64.s: What kind of State is India not, according to the philosophy of the Constitution?
64.x: Philosophy of the Constitution – Welfare state, socialist state, political equality – not a Communist State

64.s: Where is the welfare-state idea found in the Constitution?
64.x: Nature of India – A democratic polity, a sovereign State, a democratic society and a welfare state; the welfare-state idea is found in the Preamble and the DPSP

64.s: Which Preamble ideal assures both the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation?
64.x: Fraternity – Has a wider meaning than dignity of the individual alone

64.s: What is the nature of liberty in the Preamble?
64.x: Liberty – Qualified, not absolute

64.s: How many kinds of justice does the Preamble mention?
64.x: Justice – Social, economic and political – three kinds

64.s: How many kinds of liberty does the Preamble list?
64.x: Liberty – Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship – five

64.s: What sense does "Fraternity" in the Preamble denote?
64.x: Fraternity – Sense of brotherhood; assures dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation; promoted by single citizenship

64.s: Which of these is one of the goals the Preamble secures?
64.x: Goals secured to all – Justice (social, economic, political), liberty of thought and expression, equality of opportunity and dignity of the individual

64.s: Which Preamble ideal is best defined as the opportunity to develop oneself fully?
64.x: Liberty – Absence of restraints plus opportunity to develop one's personality; best defined as the opportunity to develop oneself fully (positive liberty); not licence to do whatever one likes

64.s: What does "If there are no laws, there is no liberty" treat law as?
64.x: Law and liberty – "If there are no laws, there is no liberty" – law is the condition of liberty

64.s: What is equal treatment of all with no discrimination by caste, creed or sex called?
64.x: Social justice – Equal treatment of all, equality before law, no discrimination by caste, creed or sex

64.s: Which kind of justice means equal rights to vote and hold office for all citizens?
64.x: Political justice – Political equality – equal political rights and voice

64.s: Which thinker is linked with popular sovereignty and the general will?
64.x: Political theory links – Popular/political sovereignty – Rousseau (general will); distributive justice – Aristotle

64.s: Which of these is NOT one of the Preamble's kinds of justice?
64.x: Justice – Social, economic and political – three kinds

64.s: What does political justice in the Preamble essentially mean?
64.x: Political justice – Political equality – equal political rights and voice

64.s: Which thinker is linked with distributive justice?
64.x: Distributive justice – Aristotle

64.s: When did Nehru move the Objectives Resolution that became the Preamble?
64.x: Basis – The Objectives Resolution of Jawaharlal Nehru – moved 13 December 1946, adopted 22 January 1947; its modified version became the Preamble (Nehru "proposed the Preamble"; not Ambedkar, B.N. Rau or Gandhi)

64.s: Which country's constitution was the first to begin with a Preamble?
64.x: First Preamble – The US Constitution was the first to begin with a Preamble

64.s: How many times has the Preamble been amended?
64.x: Amendments – The Preamble has been amended once

64.s: When was the third reading of the Constitution held?
64.x: Third reading of the Constitution – 17-26 November 1949; Preamble enacted last

64.s: From which country did India take the idea of a Preamble beginning "We, the people"?
64.x: Idea of a Preamble; "We, the people" – USA

64.s: From which country was the language of the Preamble taken?
64.x: Language of the Preamble – Australia

64.s: From where do the Preamble's ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity come?
64.x: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity (the "trinity"); Republic – French Revolution (1789) / French Constitution

64.s: From where does the Preamble's ideal of social, economic and political justice come?
64.x: Justice – social, economic and political – Russian Revolution (1917), USSR

64.s: Which Article of the UDHR (1948) is a possible source of "Fraternity" in the Preamble?
64.x: Fraternity (possible) – Art. 1 of the UDHR (1948)

64.s: Who called the Preamble the "identity card of the Constitution"?
64.x: "Identity card of the Constitution" – N.A. Palkhivala

64.s: Who called the Preamble the "political horoscope" of the sovereign democratic republic?
64.x: "Political horoscope" / "horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic" – K.M. Munshi

64.s: Who called the Preamble the "key-note" to the Constitution?
64.x: "Key-note" to the Constitution – Ernest Barker

64.s: Who called the Preamble the "key to the minds of the makers"?
64.x: "Key to the minds of the makers" / "key to open the mind of the makers" – Supreme Court, Berubari (1960), Sajjan Singh

64.s: Who called the Preamble the "soul" of the Constitution?
64.x: "Soul" of the Constitution – Thakurdas Bhargava (the Preamble is called the soul of the Constitution)

64.s: Which Article did Ambedkar call the "heart and soul" of the Constitution?
64.x: "Heart and soul" – Ambedkar – Article 32, not the Preamble

64.s: Who called the Preamble the "key-note" to the Constitution?
64.x: "Key of the Constitution": the standard attributions are Ernest Barker ("key-note") and the Supreme Court; no reliable source gives it to Gandhi, Motilal Nehru, Ambedkar or Indira Gandhi.

64.s: Which constitutional scholar criticised inserting "Secular" in 1976 as "productive of more mischief than benefit"?
64.x: Critic of inserting 'Secular' (1976): constitutional scholar D.D. Basu held the insertion unnecessary and productive of vagueness – "productive of more mischief than benefit".

65.s: Which Part and Articles of the Constitution contain the Fundamental Rights, the "Magna Carta of India"?
65.x: Location – Part III, Articles 12–35 of the Constitution; called the "Magna Carta of India"

65.s: Which Amendment deleted the Right to Property (Art. 31) from the Fundamental Rights?
65.x: Number – Originally seven, now six Fundamental Rights (groups) – the Right to Property (Art. 31) was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978 (Janata Party government); now a legal/constitutional right under Art. 300A (Part XII)

65.s: Which report of 1928 had demanded a bill of rights for India?
65.x: Borrowed from – The Bill of Rights of the USA; the Motilal Nehru Report (1928) had demanded a bill of rights

65.s: Why are Fundamental Rights called "fundamental"?
o: They are guaranteed and protected by the Constitution
They are granted by ordinary laws
65.x: Why "fundamental" – They are guaranteed and specifically protected by the Constitution, the fundamental law of the land – not rights granted by any ordinary law, nor merely natural-law rights

65.s: Who described the Fundamental Rights as "a pledge to our people and a pact with the civilised world"?
65.x: Description – "A pledge to our people and a pact with the civilised world" – S. Radhakrishnan

65.s: Which Articles contain the Right to Equality?
65.x: Right to Equality – 14–18 – 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination (religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth); 16 public employment; 17 untouchability abolished; 18 titles abolished

65.s: Which Article prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth?
65.x: Right to Equality – 14–18 – 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination (religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth); 16 public employment; 17 untouchability abolished; 18 titles abolished

65.s: Which Articles contain the Right to Freedom?
65.x: Right to Freedom – 19–22 – 19 six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession); 20 conviction; 21 life and personal liberty; 21A education; 22 arrest and detention

65.s: Which of these is one of the six freedoms of Art. 19?
65.x: Right to Freedom – 19–22 – 19 six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession); 20 conviction; 21 life and personal liberty; 21A education; 22 arrest and detention

65.s: Which Articles contain the Right against Exploitation?
65.x: Right against Exploitation – 23–24 – 23 traffic in human beings, forced labour; 24 child labour in factories

65.s: Which Article prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour?
65.x: Right against Exploitation – 23–24 – 23 traffic in human beings, forced labour; 24 child labour in factories

65.s: Which Articles contain the Right to Freedom of Religion?
65.x: Right to Freedom of Religion – 25–28 – Conscience, religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

65.s: Which Articles contain the Cultural and Educational Rights?
65.x: Cultural and Educational Rights – 29–30 – Minorities' culture; minorities' institutions

65.s: What do the Cultural and Educational Rights (Arts. 29-30) protect?
65.x: Cultural and Educational Rights – 29–30 – Minorities' culture; minorities' institutions

65.s: Which Article alone contains the Right to Constitutional Remedies?
65.x: Right to Constitutional Remedies – 32 alone – Writs; Art. 226 (High Courts) is outside Part III

65.s: Which writ jurisdiction lies outside Part III though it enforces rights?
65.x: Right to Constitutional Remedies – 32 alone – Writs; Art. 226 (High Courts) is outside Part III

65.s: Under which group of Fundamental Rights do Art. 15 and Art. 17 fall?
65.x: Art. 15 (prohibition of discrimination) and Art. 17 (untouchability) fall under the Right to Equality.

65.s: Which Article protects life and personal liberty?
65.x: Protection of life and personal liberty = Art. 21; Art. 20 = protection in respect of conviction; Art. 15 – discrimination, Art. 19 – association, Art. 32 – remedies.

65.s: Which of these Fundamental Rights is available to all persons, citizens and foreigners alike?
o: Art. 14 – equality before law, equal protection of laws
65.x: Art. 15 – no discrimination – Art. 14 – equality before law, equal protection of laws

65.s: Which of these Fundamental Rights is available to foreigners as well as citizens?
o: Art. 20 – protection in respect of conviction
65.x: Art. 16 – public employment – Art. 20 – protection in respect of conviction

65.s: Which of these Fundamental Rights is available to all persons, not only citizens?
65.x: Art. 19 – six freedoms (speech, movement, trade and profession…) – Art. 21 / 21A – life and liberty, education

65.s: Which of these Fundamental Rights can a (friendly) foreigner in India claim?
65.x: Art. 29 – minorities' language and culture – Art. 22 – arrest safeguards (not enemy aliens)

65.s: Which of these groups of Fundamental Rights is available to all persons, citizens and foreigners?
o: Arts. 23–24 – exploitation; Arts. 25–28 – religion; Art. 32 – remedies
65.x: Art. 30 – minorities' institutions – Arts. 23–24 – exploitation; Arts. 25–28 – religion; Art. 32 – remedies

65.s: Which right, though not a Fundamental Right, is also for citizens only?
65.x: Five citizens-only Articles – 15, 16, 19, 29, 30; also citizens only: contesting elections (not an FR at all)

65.s: Which Article's freedoms, such as speech and movement, cannot a foreigner in India claim?
65.x: A British citizen (any foreigner) in India – Cannot claim freedom of trade and profession, freedom of speech and expression, free movement or residence (all Art. 19); gets equality before law, life and liberty, religious freedom

65.s: Which right do non-citizens get along with the right to life and liberty?
65.x: Non-citizens – Get the right to life and liberty and constitutional remedies – not freedom of expression or of association (Art. 19)

65.s: Who are not given the citizens-only Fundamental Rights?
65.x: Aliens – Not given the citizens-only FRs; bankrupt or sick persons and political sufferers keep all their FRs

65.s: Which clause of Article 22 denies enemy aliens the arrest-and-detention safeguards?
65.x: Friendly and enemy aliens – The Constitution does distinguish friendly and enemy aliens – enemy aliens lose even the arrest-and-detention safeguards of Art. 22(1)-(2), by Art. 22(3)

65.s: Which Fundamental Right can companies not claim?
65.x: Companies (legal persons) – Can claim the all-persons rights, but not Art. 19

65.s: Which of these Articles is available only to citizens?
65.x: Five citizens-only Articles: 15, 16, 19, 29, 30.

65.s: Which clause takes away the arrest safeguards of Art. 22(1)-(2) from enemy aliens?
65.x: Friendly and enemy aliens – The Constitution does distinguish them – enemy aliens lose even the safeguards of Art. 22(1)-(2), by Art. 22(3)

65.s: Where in the Constitution is the right to work?
65.x: Right to work / employment – DPSP Art. 41 (not an FR)

65.s: Which DPSP provides for equal pay for equal work?
65.x: Equal pay for equal work – DPSP Art. 39(d)

65.s: Under which Article is the right to property now a legal right?
65.x: Right to property – Art. 300A, legal right since the 44th Amendment (1978)

65.s: Which Amendment lowered the voting age to 18?
65.x: Right to vote and to be elected – Constitutional right (Art. 326); given effect by statute (RPA 1950 s.19, RPA 1951 s.62); voting age lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988)

65.s: Into which Article has the Supreme Court read the right to information?
65.x: Right to information – Not listed in Part III; the Supreme Court reads it into Art. 19(1)(a) (RTI Act 2005 is a statute)

65.s: Into which Article have courts read the right to shelter?
65.x: Right to protest, right to govern, right to citizenship, right of equal shelter – Not FRs (shelter is read into Art. 21 by courts, but no "right of equal shelter" is granted)

65.s: Which Article on free education for children aged 6-14 was inserted by the 86th Amendment?
65.x: Education (6–14 years) – Art. 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002; the RTE Act enacted in 2009; both in force from 1 April 2010

65.s: Which clause gives citizens the right to settle in any part of India?
65.x: Right to settle in any part of India – Art. 19(1)(e)

65.s: Which Articles chiefly provide for gender equality?
65.x: Gender equality – Arts. 14, 15

65.s: Which Article gives the freedom to form associations and practise any profession?
65.x: Form associations, practise any profession – Art. 19

65.s: Which of these is NOT a Fundamental Right?
65.x: Of education, work, associations and profession, only the right to work is outside the Fundamental Rights.

65.s: Which Article places Fundamental Rights above ordinary laws?
65.x: Justiciable – A person can move the Supreme Court directly (Art. 32) and High Courts (Art. 226); FRs are above ordinary laws (Art. 13)

65.s: Which Article lists 11 grounds of reasonable restriction in all?
65.x: Not absolute but qualified – The State can impose reasonable restrictions by law; the courts judge reasonableness; Art. 19 lists 11 grounds of restriction in all

65.s: What are most Fundamental Rights available against?
65.x: Claimed against the State – Most FRs are available against arbitrary State action and limit the power of the State – even Parliament; some (15(2), 17, 23, 24) also bind private persons

65.s: How can Parliament curtail Fundamental Rights?
65.x: Not sacrosanct – Parliament can curtail them only by a constitutional amendment (not an ordinary law), without destroying the basic structure; they can be suspended only as the Constitution prescribes (Arts. 358-359)

65.s: Which Articles confer privileges rather than being negatively worded?
65.x: Negative and positive – Many are negatively worded (14, 15(1), 16(2), 18(1), 20, 22(1), 28(1)); 21A, 29, 30 confer privileges; 15, 17, 18, 20, 24 are absolute limits on legislative power

65.s: What is the nature of Fundamental Rights?
65.x: Nature – Both natural and legal; they protect individuals and minority groups from arbitrary State action

65.s: Which country has no written Fundamental Rights and relies on conventions and the rule of law?
65.x: Britain – No written FRs; relies on conventions and the rule of law

65.s: How many Fundamental Rights does the Constitution now guarantee?
65.x: FRs are – Not absolute; amendable; some only for citizens; drawn from the American Constitution; justiciable; six in number; granted by the Constitution; not all suspended in an emergency

65.s: Against whom are Fundamental Rights mainly enforceable?
65.x: Why fundamental – Protected and enforced by the Constitution, suspendable only as it prescribes, enforceable against the State

65.s: Which country's model does the Fundamental Rights chapter follow?
65.x: Length and model – The Constitution is the longest; the FR chapter follows the American model

65.s: Which case of 2018 held the right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia) part of Art. 21?
65.x: Right to die – Gian Kaur (1996) – no right to die (suicide) under Art. 21; Common Cause (2018) – right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia, living will) is part of Art. 21

65.s: How is India's Constitution best described?
65.x: Federal character – India is not a fully federal constitution – federal with a unitary bias ("quasi-federal")

65.s: Which Articles make up the "Golden Triangle" of the Constitution?
65.x: Golden Triangle – Arts. 14, 19 and 21 (Maneka Gandhi 1978; Minerva Mills 1980)

65.s: Who imposes reasonable restrictions on Fundamental Rights?
65.x: Reasonable restrictions are imposed by law made by Parliament (and State legislatures within their field) – not by the President, Prime Minister or Supreme Court; the courts only judge their reasonableness.

65.s: Who alone may restrict the Fundamental Rights of the armed forces and police under Art. 33?
65.x: Parliament alone may restrict or abrogate FRs of the armed forces, forces charged with maintenance of public order (police), intelligence/counter-intelligence staff, and persons in telecommunication systems set up for those forces – including non-combatants (barbers, cooks, carpenters). Examples: Army Act 1950, Air Force Act 1950, Navy Act 1957

65.s: What may Parliament pass for acts done during martial law under Art. 34?
65.x: Restrictions while martial law is in force; Parliament may pass an indemnity Act; "martial law" is not defined in the Constitution

65.s: Who alone legislates on Arts. 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34, for uniformity?
65.x: Only Parliament (not States) legislates on 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 and punishments for Part III offences – for uniformity

65.s: Which Article restricts the Fundamental Rights of the forces' own communication staff?
65.x: Staff of communication systems set up in the country in general are outside Art. 33 – they enjoy FRs at par with other citizens; only the forces' own communication staff are restricted.

65.s: On which grounds of National Emergency is Art. 19 suspended automatically?
65.x: Art. 358 – When a National Emergency is declared on war or external aggression, Art. 19 (Right to Freedom) is suspended automatically (not on armed rebellion)

65.s: Which Articles can never be suspended under Art. 359?
65.x: Art. 359 – The President may by order suspend the right to move courts for specified FRs – never Arts. 20 and 21 (44th Amendment, 1978)

65.s: Which laws does Art. 13(1) cover?
o: Laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution
65.x: 13(1) – Pre-constitution laws inconsistent with FRs are void to the extent of inconsistency – laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution (26 Jan 1950), not "before Independence"

65.s: What does Art. 13(2) bar the State from making?
o: Any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights
65.x: 13(2) – The State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges FRs; such post-constitution laws are void to that extent

65.s: Which of these is included in "law" under Art. 13(3)(a)?
o: Custom or usage having force of law
65.x: 13(3)(a) – "Law" includes ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law

65.s: Which Amendment added Art. 13(4), keeping Art. 368 amendments outside Art. 13?
65.x: 13(4) – Art. 13 does not apply to Art. 368 amendments – added by the 24th Amendment, 1971

65.s: Which Article, with Arts. 32 and 226, is the basis of judicial review?
65.x: Basis of judicial review (with Arts. 32 and 226); it gives constitutional provisions (FRs) precedence over laws of Parliament and State legislatures.

65.s: In which year was the Shankari Prasad case decided?
65.x: Shankari Prasad – 1951 – Amendment is not "law" under Art. 13; Parliament can amend FRs (first such case)

65.s: What did Shankari Prasad hold about a constitutional amendment under Art. 13?
65.x: Shankari Prasad – 1951 – Amendment is not "law" under Art. 13; Parliament can amend FRs (first such case)

65.s: In which year was the Golaknath case decided?
65.x: Golaknath – 1967 – FRs have a transcendental position – Parliament cannot abridge FRs; prospective overruling

65.s: What did Golaknath hold about Parliament's power over Fundamental Rights?
o: It can suspend them any time
It can abridge them by ordinance
65.x: Golaknath – 1967 – FRs have a transcendental position – Parliament cannot abridge FRs; prospective overruling

65.s: In which year was the 24th Amendment passed in reply to Golaknath?
65.x: 24th Amendment – 1971 – Added Art. 13(4) in reply

65.s: What did the 24th Amendment add in reply to Golaknath?
65.x: 24th Amendment – 1971 – Added Art. 13(4) in reply

65.s: What did Kesavananda Bharati hold on amending Fundamental Rights?
o: Only Parliament with States can amend them
They are amendable, but not the basic structure
65.x: Kesavananda Bharati – 1973 – FRs amendable, but the basic structure cannot be destroyed

65.s: Which Amendment added the Ninth Schedule with Arts. 31A and 31B?
65.x: Ninth Schedule: added by the 1st Amendment (1951) with Arts. 31A and 31B; I.R. Coelho (2007) – laws placed in it after 24 Apr 1973 are open to basic-structure review.

65.s: Which case held laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 open to basic-structure review?
65.x: Ninth Schedule: added by the 1st Amendment (1951) with Arts. 31A and 31B; I.R. Coelho (2007) – laws placed in it after 24 Apr 1973 are open to basic-structure review.

65.s: What happens to the consistent part of a law under the doctrine of severability?
65.x: Severability – Law is void only to the extent of inconsistency; the consistent, severable part remains valid – A.K. Gopalan (1950); R.M.D.C. (1957); Motor General Traders v. State of AP (1984)

65.s: To which laws does the doctrine of eclipse mainly apply?
65.x: Eclipse – A pre-constitution law inconsistent with an FR is not wiped out – it is dormant (overshadowed) and revives when the conflict is removed – Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP (1955); State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974) – extended to post-constitution laws for non-citizens

65.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that a person cannot waive a Fundamental Right?
65.x: Waiver – A person cannot waive an FR – Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959)

65.s: What is prospective overruling?
o: A ruling that needs Parliament's assent
A ruling that operates only for the future
A ruling binding only on States
65.x: Prospective overruling – A ruling operates only for the future – Golaknath (1967)

65.s: In which case was the doctrine of prospective overruling applied?
65.x: Prospective overruling – A ruling operates only for the future – Golaknath (1967)

65.s: Which doctrine treats the Constitution as a living document?
65.x: Progressive interpretation – Constitution as a living document – Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Art. 21; SaveLIFE Foundation v. UoI (2026) – right to trauma care under Art. 21

65.s: Which 1978 case widened the scope of Art. 21 through progressive interpretation?
65.x: Progressive interpretation – Constitution as a living document – Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Art. 21; SaveLIFE Foundation v. UoI (2026) – right to trauma care under Art. 21

65.s: Under which doctrine is a hazardous industry liable without any exceptions?
65.x: Absolute liability – Hazardous industry liable without exceptions – M.C. Mehta (1987) – Oleum gas leak

65.s: In which case did the Supreme Court lay down absolute liability after the Oleum gas leak?
65.x: Absolute liability – Hazardous industry liable without exceptions – M.C. Mehta (1987) – Oleum gas leak

65.s: In which case was the doctrine of territorial nexus applied?
65.x: Territorial nexus – State law can operate outside the State if there is sufficient connection – State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957)

65.s: Which doctrine looks at the true nature of a law when it encroaches on another List?
65.x: Pith and substance – Encroachment on another List – look at the true nature of the law – Federal doctrine (with aspect, colourable legislation, incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy)

65.s: Under which doctrine does an inconsistent law sleep and revive when the conflict is removed?
65.x: Eclipse vs severability: eclipse = law sleeps and revives; severability = bad part cut off, rest lives. Eminent domain and pleasure are unrelated doctrines.

65.s: Which of these is included in "the State" under Art. 12?
65.x: "The State" includes – Government and Parliament of India; Government and Legislature of each State; all local authorities (municipalities, panchayats, district boards); other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India (LIC, ONGC, electricity boards)

65.s: In which case was the judiciary held not to be "State" in its judicial function?
65.x: Ambiguity – courts – Whether the judiciary is "other authority" is the grey area; in its judicial function it is not "State" (Naresh Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra, 1967)

65.s: When can a writ lie against a private body doing a public activity?
65.x: Private bodies – A writ does not ordinarily lie merely because a private body performs a public activity, unless the State is involved

65.s: In which year did Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal hold statutory bodies to be "other authorities"?
65.x: Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal – 1967 – Statutory bodies are "other authorities"

65.s: What did Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal hold about statutory bodies?
65.x: Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal – 1967 – Statutory bodies are "other authorities"
