68.s: Which case upheld a mentally challenged woman's right to bear a child?
68.x: Mentally retarded woman's right to bear a child – Suchita Srivastava (2009)

68.s: Whose rights have courts read into Art. 21 besides protection against torture and solitary confinement?
68.x: Also under Art. 21: rights of craniopagus (conjoined) twins; protection against torture and solitary confinement.

68.s: Which 2023 case found no unqualified fundamental right to marry?
68.x: Marriage: Art. 21 protects the choice of partner, but Supriyo Chakraborty (2023) found no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such; travel abroad is an FR (Maneka).

68.s: What was the majority by which privacy was held a Fundamental Right in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)?
68.x: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 – Nine-judge bench, unanimous (9:0) – privacy is a Fundamental Right, an intrinsic part of Article 21 and the freedoms of Part III

68.s: In which year was M.P. Sharma, overruled in Puttaswamy on privacy, decided?
68.x: Overruled – M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962), to the extent they denied privacy as an FR

68.s: Which three-part test did Puttaswamy lay down for limiting privacy?
68.x: Test for limiting privacy – Legality (a law), legitimate aim, proportionality

68.s: What right does an arrested person have under Art. 22(1)?
o: To be told the grounds and to consult a lawyer
68.x: Rights of the arrested – Told the grounds of arrest; may consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice

68.s: How many hours does the police have to produce an arrested person before a magistrate under Art. 22(2)?
68.x: Art. 22(2) – Produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours (excluding journey time)

68.s: Who are excluded from the arrest safeguards of Art. 22(1)-(2)?
68.x: 22(3) exclusions – Enemy aliens and persons held under a preventive detention law – ordinary foreigners and OCIs are covered; detention beyond 24 hours without a magistrate only in preventive detention

68.s: Which of these arrests falls outside the safeguards of Art. 22(1)-(2)?
o: Police arrest for a cognisable offence
68.x: Also outside – Arrest on a court order (person in jail under judicial order), civil arrest, deportation of an alien

68.s: Which of these is not guaranteed to an arrested person under Art. 22?
68.x: Not guaranteed – Bail as of right, trial by jury

68.s: Which BNSS sections replaced CrPC Secs. 50 and 57 on arrest?
68.x: Statute – CrPC Secs. 50, 57 → BNSS Secs. 47, 58

68.s: Which 2025 case held that grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee?
o: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana
68.x: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (2025) – Grounds must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee

68.s: What is preventive detention?
o: Detention without trial on suspicion of future harm
68.x: Preventive detention – Without trial, on suspicion of future harmful acts; justified for public order, not routine law and order

68.s: What is punitive detention?
68.x: Punitive detention – After trial and conviction

68.s: What is the longest a person can be preventively detained without an Advisory Board's report under Art. 22(4)?
68.x: 22(4) – No detention beyond 3 months unless an Advisory Board (High Court judges or persons qualified to be) reports sufficient cause

68.s: To what period did the 44th Amendment cut detention without an Advisory Board, a clause never notified?
68.x: 44th Amendment (1978) – Cut it to 2 months, but the clause was never notified – 3 months still applies

68.s: What does Art. 22(5) give a preventive detenu?
o: Grounds and the earliest opportunity of representation
68.x: 22(5) – Grounds communicated + earliest opportunity of representation

68.s: Who fixes the maximum period of preventive detention under Art. 22(7)?
68.x: 22(7) – Parliament fixes the maximum period and the Advisory Board procedure

68.s: On which subjects can only Parliament make preventive detention laws?
o: Defence, foreign affairs, security of India
68.x: Parliament alone – Defence, foreign affairs, security of India

68.s: On which subjects can both Parliament and States make preventive detention laws?
o: Public order, security of a State, essential supplies
68.x: Parliament and States – Public order, security of a State, essential supplies

68.s: In which year was India's first Preventive Detention Act passed?
68.x: Preventive Detention Act – 1950 – First such law; lapsed 1969

68.s: When did the Preventive Detention Act of 1950 lapse?
68.x: Preventive Detention Act – 1950 – First such law; lapsed 1969

68.s: In which year was the UAPA enacted?
68.x: UAPA – 1967 – Anti-terror; SC (Jan 2026): delay alone not a "trump card" for bail

68.s: What did the Supreme Court hold in January 2026 about delay in UAPA cases?
o: UAPA trials must end in 6 months
Delay alone is not a trump card for bail
68.x: UAPA – 1967 – Anti-terror; SC (Jan 2026): delay alone not a "trump card" for bail

68.s: In which year was MISA enacted?
68.x: MISA – 1971 – Enacted under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi; widely used in the Emergency (1975-77); repealed 1978

68.s: Under which Prime Minister was MISA enacted?
68.x: MISA – 1971 – Enacted under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi; widely used in the Emergency (1975-77); repealed 1978

68.s: In which year was COFEPOSA enacted?
68.x: COFEPOSA – 1974 – Smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators

68.s: Against whom is COFEPOSA directed?
68.x: COFEPOSA – 1974 – Smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators

68.s: In which year was the National Security Act enacted?
68.x: NSA – 1980 – Detention up to 12 months without charges

68.s: How long can a person be detained without charges under the NSA?
68.x: NSA – 1980 – Detention up to 12 months without charges

68.s: From which country's Constitution does "procedure established by law" in Art. 21 come?
68.x: Text: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law" – the phrase comes from the Japanese Constitution; "due process of law" is American and is not used in Art. 21.

68.s: What kind of procedure did Maneka Gandhi (1978) require under Art. 21?
68.x: Any procedure enacted by the legislature suffices – Procedure must be just, fair and reasonable

68.s: What does Art. 21 protect against after Maneka Gandhi, besides executive action?
68.x: Protects only against the executive – Also against arbitrary legislation – in effect American due process read into Art. 21

68.s: What is "due process of law" in essence?
68.x: Due process of law – In essence the principle of natural justice; now read into Article 21

68.s: What does audi alteram partem mean?
o: No one a judge in his own cause
68.x: Audi alteram partem – "Hear the other side" – the right to be heard

68.s: What does nemo judex in causa sua mean?
o: The law does not concern trifles
No one a judge in his own cause
68.x: *Nemo judex in causa sua* – No one a judge in his own cause

68.s: Which case of 2023 held Arts. 19 and 21 enforceable against private persons too?
o: Kaushal Kishor v. State of UP
68.x: Protection against – The State's executive and legislative action; since Kaushal Kishor v. State of UP, 2023, Arts. 19 and 21 can also be enforced against private persons

68.s: Which Article does unguided, uncontrolled executive discretion break?
68.x: Unguided, uncontrolled executive discretion – Breaks Article 14 (arbitrary)

68.s: Which case upheld capital punishment under the "rarest of rare" doctrine?
68.x: Capital punishment – Does not violate Art. 21 – Bachan Singh (1980), "rarest of rare"

68.s: In which year did the Bombay HC in Maruti Shripati Dubal hold the right to die part of Art. 21?
68.x: Maruti Shripati Dubal (Bombay HC) – 1987 – Right to die part of Art. 21; Sec. 309 IPC unconstitutional

68.s: What did the Bombay HC hold in Maruti Shripati Dubal (1987)?
o: Right to education flows from Art. 21
Right to die is part of Art. 21
68.x: Maruti Shripati Dubal (Bombay HC) – 1987 – Right to die part of Art. 21; Sec. 309 IPC unconstitutional

68.s: In which year did the AP High Court in Chenna Jagadeeswar uphold Sec. 309 IPC?
68.x: Chenna Jagadeeswar (AP High Court) – 1988 – Art. 21 gives no right to die; Sec. 309 upheld

68.s: What did the AP High Court hold in Chenna Jagadeeswar (1988)?
o: Art. 21 gives a right to die
Art. 21 gives no right to die; Sec. 309 upheld
68.x: Chenna Jagadeeswar (AP High Court) – 1988 – Art. 21 gives no right to die; Sec. 309 upheld

68.s: In which year did P. Rathinam hold Sec. 309 IPC unconstitutional?
68.x: P. Rathinam – 1994 – Sec. 309 IPC (attempted suicide) unconstitutional

68.s: What did P. Rathinam (1994) hold about attempted suicide under Sec. 309 IPC?
68.x: P. Rathinam – 1994 – Sec. 309 IPC (attempted suicide) unconstitutional

68.s: In which year did Gian Kaur overrule P. Rathinam?
68.x: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab – 1996 – Overruled Rathinam: "right to life" does not include "right to die" (only a right to die with dignity); Sec. 309 valid

68.s: In which year did the Supreme Court decide the Aruna Shanbaug case on euthanasia?
68.x: Aruna Shanbaug – 2011 – Nurse in a vegetative state for 42 years after a 1973 assault – face of the euthanasia debate; plea rejected, but passive euthanasia under High Court supervision allowed

68.s: How long was Aruna Shanbaug in a vegetative state?
68.x: Aruna Shanbaug – 2011 – Nurse in a vegetative state for 42 years after a 1973 assault – face of the euthanasia debate; plea rejected, but passive euthanasia under High Court supervision allowed

68.s: In which year did Common Cause uphold the right to die with dignity?
68.x: Common Cause – 2018 – Dying with dignity an FR under Art. 21; living will / advance directive upheld

68.s: What did Common Cause (2018) uphold along with dying with dignity?
68.x: Common Cause – 2018 – Dying with dignity an FR under Art. 21; living will / advance directive upheld

68.s: Which law of 2017 effectively decriminalised attempted suicide?
o: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act
68.x: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 – Attempted suicide effectively decriminalised

68.s: Which law: No general offence of attempted suicide?
68.x: BNS, 2023 (in force 1 July 2024) – No general offence of attempted suicide

68.s: Which Amendment barred suspension of Arts. 20 and 21 even in a National Emergency?
68.x: 44th Amendment (1978): the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Art. 359, even during a National Emergency – the only such FRs (Arts. 14, 19, 22 can be).

68.s: Which Article's freedoms of movement, residence and profession can be suspended in an emergency?
68.x: The "right to life and personal liberty" can never be suspended; freedom of movement, residence and profession (Art. 19) can.

69.s: In which year was the 44th Amendment, which deleted the right to property, enacted?
69.x: Amendment – The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 deleted the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights

69.s: Which clause on acquiring, holding and disposing of property was omitted along with Art. 31?
69.x: Articles omitted – Art. 19(1)(f) (acquire, hold and dispose of property) and Art. 31 (compulsory acquisition), taken out of Part III

69.s: In which Part of the Constitution is Art. 300A placed?
69.x: New Article – Art. 300A in Part XII (Chapter IV)

69.s: Which government passed the 44th Amendment deleting the right to property?
69.x: Government – The Janata Party government of Morarji Desai (1977-79)

69.s: From which date did the omission of Art. 31 take effect, ending property as a Fundamental Right?
69.x: Date – The Act is "of 1978"; assent on 30 April 1979; the omission of Art. 31 (s.6) took effect from 20 June 1979 – property ceased to be an FR from 1979

69.s: Why was the right to property removed from the Fundamental Rights?
69.x: Why – Property rights were the most litigated FR and kept blocking land reform and acquisition for public use

69.s: How many Fundamental Rights were there originally?
69.x: Result – FRs originally seven, now six; property is the only FR ever deleted

69.s: Which Article says "No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law"?
69.x: Text – "No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law" – bars the State from taking property except by law

69.s: Which Article deals with suits by and against the Government?
69.x: Neighbouring Articles – Art. 299 = contracts; Art. 300 = suits by/against Government; Art. 301 = freedom of trade

69.s: What kind of right is the right to property under Art. 300A?
69.x: Status – A legal right (also called a constitutional right, since it is in the Constitution); not a Fundamental Right, DPSP or natural right

69.s: Who can claim the right under Art. 300A?
69.x: Who – Any person – citizens, non-citizens and companies

69.s: Through which remedy is the right under Art. 300A enforced?
69.x: Enforcement – Through Art. 226 or an ordinary suit, not Art. 32; protects against executive action without law, not against legislation; no constitutional duty to pay compensation

69.s: Which Article of the UDHR (1948) recognises the right to property?
69.x: Human right – The Supreme Court has repeatedly held property is also a human right (forcible dispossession without due process = human-rights violation); UDHR 1948 Art. 17 recognises it

69.s: Which case held that the right to property is not part of the basic structure?
69.x: Basic structure – Kesavananda Bharati (1973): the right to property is not part of the basic structure

69.s: What did the AP High Court insist on in GGR Housing v. State (May 2026)?
o: Strict statutory due process in land acquisition
69.x: GGR Housing v. State (AP High Court, May 2026) – Strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Art. 300A

69.s: What does Article 300A protect property against?
69.x: Protection – Against executive action without law, not against legislation; the State is not constitutionally bound to pay compensation

69.s: Who has the right under Art. 29(1) to conserve a distinct language, script or culture?
69.x: 29(1) – Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it (not limited to minorities)

69.s: Which ground is NOT listed in Art. 29(2) for denial of admission?
69.x: 29(2) – No citizen denied admission to a State-maintained or State-aided institution on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language (sex and place of birth are not in the list)

69.s: What is the marginal heading of Art. 29?
69.x: Marginal heading – Art. 29 = "Protection of interests of minorities"

69.s: What is the objective of the Cultural and Educational Rights?
o: To help minorities conserve their culture
69.x: Objective of the group – To help minorities conserve their culture

69.s: Which Article's text is not confined to citizens, unlike Art. 29?
69.x: Scope – Art. 29 applies to citizens only; Art. 30's text is not confined to citizens

69.s: Which minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice under Art. 30(1)?
69.x: 30(1) – All minorities, religious or linguistic, may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice – the "Charter of Education Rights"; madrasas run under it

69.s: Which Amendment added clause 30(1A) on acquiring a minority institution's property?
69.x: 30(1A) (44th Amendment, 1978) – On compulsory acquisition of a minority institution's property, the amount fixed must not restrict or abrogate the Art. 30 right

69.s: Which clause bars discrimination in grant of aid to an institution under minority management?
69.x: 30(2) – No discrimination in grant of aid because an institution is under minority management

69.s: What may the State not do while regulating minority institutions under Art. 30?
69.x: Art. 30 is not absolute: the State may regulate standards, but may not take away the minority character ("right to administer is not a right to maladminister").

69.s: Which Article gives the right to propagate religion?
69.x: Spreading religion (propagation) is Art. 25 – a right of all persons, minorities included.

69.s: Whose children must get instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage under Art. 350A?
69.x: Art. 350A – Every State and local authority to provide instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage to children of linguistic minority groups

69.s: Which officer does Art. 350B provide for?
69.x: Art. 350B – Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities

69.s: Which minorities may establish and administer educational institutions under Art. 30?
69.x: Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions; minorities may spread their religion; religious minorities are not defined in Art. 350A.

69.s: Which statement is correct?
o: Legal rights cannot be changed by ordinary law
Every human right is an FR
Every constitutional right is an FR
Every FR is a constitutional right, but not the reverse
69.x: Every FR is a constitutional right, but not every constitutional right is an FR; a legal right comes from ordinary law and can be changed by it; every FR is a human right, but not the reverse.

69.s: What kind of right is the right to vote and be elected?
69.x: Vote and to be elected – Constitutional right – Art. 326 (adult suffrage, 18+); Sec. 62 RPA 1951; registration Sec. 19 RPA 1950

69.s: Which section of the RPA 1951 deals with the right to vote?
69.x: Vote and to be elected – Constitutional right – Art. 326 (adult suffrage, 18+); Sec. 62 RPA 1951; registration Sec. 19 RPA 1950

69.s: Into which Article does the Supreme Court read the right to information?
69.x: Information – Legal right under the RTI Act, 2005; the Supreme Court also reads it into Art. 19(1)(a) – RTI Act 2005; Art. 19(1)(a)

69.s: What is the status of the right to work?
69.x: Work – DPSP – Art. 41

69.s: What is the status of the right to education for children aged 6-14?
69.x: Education (6-14) – Fundamental Right – Art. 21A

69.s: Where is Education (6-14)?
69.x: Education (6-14) – Fundamental Right – Art. 21A

69.s: Which case held that voting is only a statutory right?
o: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India
69.x: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2009): voting is only a statutory/legal right.

69.s: Under which Article are the voter's right to know candidates, NOTA and ballot secrecy recognised?
69.x: Voting paradox: voting is statutory, yet the right to know candidate details, NOTA and ballot secrecy are recognised under Art. 19(1)(a).

69.s: In which Articles is "minority" used but not defined?
69.x: Not defined – "Minority" is used in Arts. 29, 30, 350A, 350B but not defined in the Constitution; there is no 10% or 10,000 population test

69.s: Under which Act is a "minority" a community notified by the Central Government?
69.x: NCM Act, 1992 – "Minority" = a community notified by the Central Government; the NCM is a statutory body (quasi-judicial, civil-court powers), not constitutional

69.s: Which case held that minorities are to be determined State-wise?
69.x: Unit = the State – Religious and linguistic minorities determined State-wise (T.M.A. Pai, 2002); tests: numerical inferiority, non-dominance, distinct identity

69.s: At which level are religious minorities notified by the NCM and Minority Affairs Ministry?
69.x: Religious minority – NCM, Ministry of Minority Affairs – national notification

69.s: How is a linguistic minority determined?
69.x: Linguistic minority – State-wise

69.s: In which year were Jains notified as a minority community?
69.x: Six notified minorities – Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains (Jains added 2014); linguistic minorities are not among these religious categories

69.s: Which central scheme for minorities is brought into reach by national notification?
69.x: National notification – Brings a group within the NCM and central schemes (scholarships, PMJVK, PM VIKAS)

69.s: Which linguistic minority in Kasaragod contested Kerala's Malayalam Bhasha Bill in 2026?
69.x: Mar 2026 – Kerala's Malayalam Bhasha Bill contested as harming the Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod

69.s: When did the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 come into force?
69.x: 1894 Act – Made by the British; in force 1 March 1894; purpose not land reform but acquisition for public purposes, institutions and companies; disputed and replaced by the LARR Act, 2013

69.s: What is the maximum compensation, as a multiple of market value, in rural areas under the LARR Act, 2013?
69.x: LARR Act, 2013 – Social Impact Assessment compulsory; compensation up to 4x market value (rural), 2x (urban); unused land returned after 5 years

69.s: Who keeps enemy property in India, which is not returned to the legal heirs of the enemy owner?
69.x: Enemy property stays vested in the Custodian; the law of succession/inheritance does not apply to it and no legal heir can claim it – it is not returned to heirs.

69.s: Under which clause was the right to property a Fundamental Right in 1950, alongside Article 31?
69.x: 1950 – FR under Art. 19(1)(f) + Art. 31 – the most disputed FR

69.s: Which Amendment of 1951 added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield land-reform laws?
69.x: 1st Amendment, 1951 – Arts. 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield land-reform laws

69.s: What must be paid, under the 17th Amendment (1964), to acquire land under personal cultivation?
69.x: 4th (1955), 17th (1964), 25th (1971) – Narrowed compensation; 17th: land under personal cultivation acquired only on paying market value

69.s: Which Amendment deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and inserted Article 300A?
69.x: 44th Amendment, 1978 – Deleted 19(1)(f) and 31 → Art. 300A

69.s: Which saving clause, added in 1951, protects laws on the acquisition of estates?
69.x: 31A – 1st, 1951 – Laws on acquisition of estates etc.

69.s: Which saving clause makes the Acts in the Ninth Schedule immune from Fundamental Rights challenge?
69.x: 31B – 1st, 1951 – Acts in the Ninth Schedule – immune from FR challenge

69.s: In which case was the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles struck down?
69.x: 31C – 25th, 1971 – Laws giving effect to Arts. 39(b), 39(c); the 42nd's extension to all DPSPs struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)

69.s: After which date must Ninth Schedule laws be inserted to be open to basic structure review (I.R. Coelho, 2007)?
69.x: I.R. Coelho (2007), 9 judges: Ninth Schedule laws inserted after 24 April 1973 are open to basic structure review.

69.s: In which year did the Supreme Court decide the St. Stephen's College minority-institution case?
69.x: St. Stephen's College – 1992 – Minority-institution autonomy (5-judge bench)

69.s: Which 1992 case of a 5-judge bench upheld the autonomy of a minority institution, a Delhi college?
69.x: St. Stephen's College – 1992 – Minority-institution autonomy (5-judge bench)

69.s: In which 2002 case did an 11-judge bench hold that minority status is decided State-wise?
69.x: T.M.A. Pai Foundation – 2002 – 11-judge bench; minority status decided State-wise

69.s: Which Amendment followed the P.A. Inamdar ruling (2005) against State quotas in unaided colleges?
69.x: P.A. Inamdar – 2005 – 7 judges; no State reservation in unaided private colleges → led to the 93rd Amendment (Art. 15(5), which exempts minority institutions)

69.s: In which year did the Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust judgment come?
69.x: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust – 2014 – RTE Act's 25% quota does not apply to minority schools

69.s: Which 2014 judgment held that the RTE Act's 25% quota does not apply to minority schools?
69.x: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust – 2014 – RTE Act's 25% quota does not apply to minority schools

69.s: In which year was St. Xavier's College (Ahmedabad) v. State of Gujarat decided?
69.x: St. Xavier's College (Ahmedabad) v. State of Gujarat – 1974 – Nine-judge bench – the State may regulate standards but cannot control the management of a minority college

69.s: What size of bench decided St. Xavier's College (Ahmedabad) v. State of Gujarat (1974)?
69.x: St. Xavier's College (Ahmedabad) v. State of Gujarat – 1974 – Nine-judge bench – the State may regulate standards but cannot control the management of a minority college

70.s: How many writs does Article 32(2) name?
70.x: Article 32(2) – Names five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto (an injunction is not one of them)

70.s: Under which Article does the Supreme Court issue writs, as the High Courts do under Article 226?
70.x: Issuing courts – Both the Supreme Court (Art. 32) and the High Courts (Art. 226) issue all five

70.s: Which High Courts alone could issue prerogative writs before 1950?
70.x: Origin – Prerogative writs of English common law; before 1950 only the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts could issue them

70.s: Which writ literally means "to have the body (of)"?
70.x: Habeas Corpus – "To have the body (of)" / "you may have the body" – Detained person produced before the court; release from illegal detention; court inquires into the legality of detention – Public authorities and private individuals

70.s: Against whom does the writ of Habeas Corpus lie?
70.x: Habeas Corpus – "To have the body (of)" / "you may have the body" – Detained person produced before the court; release from illegal detention; court inquires into the legality of detention – Public authorities and private individuals

70.s: Which writ literally means "we command"?
70.x: Mandamus – "We command" (an order) – Orders a public official, body, inferior court or government to perform a public duty it refused or neglected; can also order it not to enforce an unconstitutional law – Public officials, statutory bodies, government companies, inferior courts, tribunals, government

70.s: Which writ, besides ordering a public duty, can order an authority not to enforce an unconstitutional law?
70.x: Mandamus – "We command" (an order) – Orders a public official, body, inferior court or government to perform a public duty it refused or neglected; can also order it not to enforce an unconstitutional law – Public officials, statutory bodies, government companies, inferior courts, tribunals, government

70.s: Which writ literally means "to forbid"?
70.x: Prohibition – "To forbid" / restrain – Higher court stops a lower court/tribunal exceeding its jurisdiction while the case is pending – Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only

70.s: Which writ stops a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction while a case is still pending?
70.x: Prohibition – "To forbid" / restrain – Higher court stops a lower court/tribunal exceeding its jurisdiction while the case is pending – Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only

70.s: Against whom does the writ of Prohibition lie?
70.x: Prohibition – "To forbid" / restrain – Higher court stops a lower court/tribunal exceeding its jurisdiction while the case is pending – Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only

70.s: Which writ literally means "to be certified" or informed?
70.x: Certiorari – "To be certified" / informed – Higher court calls up the record of a lower court/tribunal for review; quashes an order already passed; also transfers a pending case – Judicial, quasi-judicial and (since 1991) certain administrative bodies

70.s: Which writ lets a higher court quash an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal?
70.x: Certiorari – "To be certified" / informed – Higher court calls up the record of a lower court/tribunal for review; quashes an order already passed; also transfers a pending case – Judicial, quasi-judicial and (since 1991) certain administrative bodies

70.s: Which writ ousts a person who holds a public office without the right to it?
70.x: Quo Warranto – "By what authority (or warrant)?" / "what is your authority" – Court asks a holder to show his right to a public office; ousts an ineligible person / usurper – Holder of a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution

70.s: Which writ, the "bulwark of individual liberty", also produces a person missing or in custody?
70.x: Habeas Corpus – The writ of personal liberty – the "bulwark of individual liberty", the greatest safeguard of personal liberty; also produces a person missing or in custody; the term belongs to law

70.s: Which writ: Judiciary orders the Executive to perform its duty – "an order to act legally and abstain from an unlawful act"?
70.x: Mandamus – Judiciary orders the Executive to perform its duty – "an order to act legally and abstain from an unlawful act"

70.s: Which writ is called the "postmortem" writ, as it examines orders of subordinate courts already passed?
70.x: Certiorari – The "postmortem" writ – examines the working of subordinate courts; sought to get an order quashed; grounds: lack/excess of jurisdiction, error of law on the face of the record

70.s: Which writ directs inactivity, i.e. stops a lower court from proceeding?
70.x: Mandamus directs activity; Prohibition directs inactivity. Certifying proceedings is Certiorari; producing the body is Habeas Corpus.

70.s: Which writ directs activity, commanding a public authority to perform its duty?
70.x: Mandamus directs activity; Prohibition directs inactivity. Certifying proceedings is Certiorari; producing the body is Habeas Corpus.

70.s: Which Article gives the right to move the Supreme Court directly when a Fundamental Right is violated?
70.x: Right to Constitutional Remedies – Article 32 – the right to move the Supreme Court directly when a Fundamental Right is violated; itself a Fundamental Right

70.s: What would the Constitution be without Article 32, according to Ambedkar?
70.x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar – Art. 32 is "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" – without it the Constitution would be a nullity

70.s: What is a right without a remedy, the reason Article 32 was made a Fundamental Right?
70.x: Why – "A right without a remedy is a worthless declaration" – Art. 32 gives an effective remedy against violation of FRs

70.s: Which Article did Ambedkar call "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it"?
70.x: "Soul" alone – Also used for the Preamble (Thakur Das Bhargava); with Ambedkar or "heart and soul" it is Art. 32 / Right to Constitutional Remedies

70.s: Under which Article is the Supreme Court's judicial review part of the inviolable basic structure?
70.x: Basic structure – Judicial review under Art. 32 (SC) and Arts. 226 and 227 (HCs) is part of the inviolable basic structure – Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges); L. Chandra Kumar (1997); Art. 245 is not

70.s: Through which Article does the Supreme Court exercise its power of judicial review to enforce FRs?
70.x: SC's power of judicial review – Exercised through Art. 32

70.s: Which pair of Articles is the clearest expression of judicial review in India?
70.x: Clearest expression – Arts. 32 and 226

70.s: Besides Arts. 32 and 226, which Article is a basis of judicial review in India?
70.x: Basis – Arts. 13, 32, 226; Art. 225 (jurisdiction of existing HCs) is not a basis

70.s: Where can citizens move for infringement of a Fundamental Right?
o: The Supreme Court or the High Court
70.x: Infringement of FRs – Citizens move the Supreme Court (Art. 32) or the High Court (Art. 226)

70.s: Which courts alone can issue writs in India?
70.x: Who issues writs – Only the SC and HCs – not other courts, Parliament or the President

70.s: Which Article empowers the High Courts to issue writs?
70.x: Article 226 – Empowers the High Courts to issue writs

70.s: Which organ is the guardian and protector of Fundamental Rights?
70.x: Guardian / protector of Fundamental Rights – The Judiciary (Supreme Court as "protector and guarantor") – not the President, Parliament, Executive, Cabinet or parties

70.s: Which institution is the custodian of the Constitution?
70.x: Supreme Court – Also the custodian / guardian of the Constitution

70.s: What is the nature of the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction, since HCs also decide the validity of Central laws?
70.x: SC's writ power – Original but not exclusive; HCs also decide the validity of Central laws

70.s: Under which Article is the writ remedy itself a Fundamental Right, so it cannot be refused when an FR is shown?
70.x: Nature – Itself a Fundamental Right – SC cannot refuse when an FR is shown – Constitutional, discretionary remedy

70.s: Under which Article is the writ remedy a constitutional but discretionary remedy?
70.x: Nature – Itself a Fundamental Right – SC cannot refuse when an FR is shown – Constitutional, discretionary remedy

70.s: Which Article's writ power covers only Fundamental Rights, the narrower scope?
70.x: Scope – Only Fundamental Rights (narrower) – FRs and "any other purpose" – constitutional and statutory (legal) rights (wider)

70.s: Which Article lets High Courts issue writs for FRs and for "any other purpose"?
70.x: Scope – Only Fundamental Rights (narrower) – FRs and "any other purpose" – constitutional and statutory (legal) rights (wider)

70.s: Over which territory does the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32 extend?
70.x: Territory – Whole of India (wider) – Own territory; beyond it if the cause of action arises inside (15th Amendment, 1963)

70.s: Which Amendment let a High Court issue writs beyond its territory if the cause of action arises inside?
70.x: Territory – Whole of India (wider) – Own territory; beyond it if the cause of action arises inside (15th Amendment, 1963)

70.s: How many kinds of writs can the Supreme Court issue under Article 32?
70.x: Writs – Five – Five

70.s: Why are the High Courts in a better position to protect citizens' rights than the SC?
70.x: High Courts are in a better position to protect citizens' rights, because the SC issues writs only for FRs; the HC writ power covers constitutional, statutory and fundamental rights.

70.s: Under which Article is a non-fundamental right such as the right to vote enforced?
70.x: A right that is not an FR – e.g. the right to vote – is enforced in the High Court under Art. 226, not Art. 32.

70.s: In which 1957 case was it held that Art. 226 relief is refused where an alternative remedy exists?
70.x: Art. 226 is ordinarily refused where an alternative and equally efficacious remedy exists (rule of prudence; T.R. Verma 1957) or where disputed questions of fact need trial; it is not barred merely because no FR is involved ("any other purpose").

70.s: Under which Article does the Supreme Court review its own judgment?
70.x: Art. 137 – SC reviews its own judgment

70.s: Which Article is the basis for the Supreme Court declaring a law unconstitutional for violating FRs?
70.x: Art. 13 – SC declares a law unconstitutional

70.s: What kind of High Court dismissal bars the same plea under Article 32 by res judicata?
70.x: Res judicata – An HC dismissal on merits bars the same plea under Art. 32 (remedy: appeal)

70.s: When in 2026 did the SC agree to examine whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction?
70.x: 20 Jan 2026 – SC (Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma) agreed to examine whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction (appeals by Kerala and Tamil Nadu)

70.s: When in 2026 did the SC study an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings under Arts. 32 and 226?
70.x: 16 Jul 2026 – SC studied an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings under Arts. 32 and 226 in threats to life and liberty

70.s: In which year did the 42nd Amendment insert Article 32A and curb Article 226?
70.x: 42nd – 1976 – Inserted Art. 32A (no challenge to State laws under Art. 32); curbed Art. 226

70.s: In which year did the 43rd Amendment omit Article 32A?
70.x: 43rd – 1977 – Omitted Arts. 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A, 228A

70.s: Which Amendment omitted Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A?
70.x: 43rd – 1977 – Omitted Arts. 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A, 228A

70.s: In which year did the 44th Amendment restore Article 226?
70.x: 44th – 1978 – Restored Art. 226

70.s: Which Amendment restored the High Courts' writ power under Article 226 after the 42nd had curbed it?
70.x: 44th – 1978 – Restored Art. 226

70.s: Which writ safeguards the liberty of all persons in the territory, citizens or not, and lies even against private persons?
70.x: Reach – The only writ that lies against private persons as well as the State; safeguards the liberty of all persons in the territory, citizens or not

70.s: When is Habeas Corpus not issued?
o: When detention is by the police
When the detenu is a foreigner
When detention is by a private person
70.x: Not issued – Where detention is lawful, by a competent court (judicial custody), for contempt of court/legislature, or outside the court's territory

70.s: Which writ petition is not dismissed merely for imperfect pleadings?
70.x: Pleadings – A petition is not dismissed for imperfect pleadings

70.s: Which writ lies against public officials and government companies to compel performance of public duties?
70.x: Lies against – Public officials, government, public corporations and government companies performing public duties, inferior courts and tribunals

70.s: Under which Article does Mandamus not lie against the President or Governors?
70.x: Does not lie against – A private individual or body (unless entrusted with a public duty or colluding with a public authority); the President or Governors (Art. 361); a contractual obligation; a discretionary duty; non-statutory instructions; a Chief Justice acting judicially

70.s: Which writ cannot compel the Government to make a law or policy, but enforces a policy once laid down?
70.x: Law and policy – Mandamus cannot compel the Government to make a law or a policy (e.g. to appoint a commission to study climate change), but enforces a policy once laid down

70.s: Which writ orders an authority to fill vacant seats or build cyclone shelters as a public duty?
70.x: Public duties – It lies to compel statutory/public duties (filling seats, cleanliness, cyclone shelters)

70.s: Which bodies alone can be stopped by the writ of Prohibition?
70.x: Prohibition – Only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies – not administrative authorities, legislatures, private persons; it goes to the lower court

70.s: Which bodies affecting rights can also be reached by Certiorari since 1991?
70.x: Certiorari – Not against legislative bodies or private persons; since 1991 also against administrative bodies affecting rights

70.s: Who may seek a writ of Quo Warranto, without having to be aggrieved?
70.x: Quo Warranto – Any public-minded person may seek it (need not be aggrieved); not for a ministerial or private office

70.s: At what stage is the writ of Prohibition issued?
70.x: Stage – While proceedings are pending – After an order is passed (also transfers a pending case)

70.s: At what stage is the writ of Certiorari issued?
70.x: Stage – While proceedings are pending – After an order is passed (also transfers a pending case)

70.s: What is the nature of the writ of Prohibition?
70.x: Nature – Preventive only – Preventive and curative

70.s: What is the nature of the writ of Certiorari?
70.x: Nature – Preventive only – Preventive and curative

70.s: Which writ, like Certiorari, traditionally lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies?
70.x: Similarity: both lie (traditionally) only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies; both check excess of jurisdiction; both are issued by the SC and HCs.

70.s: Which clause of Article 32 guarantees the right to move the SC for enforcement of Part III rights?
70.x: 32(1) – Right to move the SC by appropriate proceedings for enforcement of Part III rights – itself guaranteed

70.s: Which clause of Article 32 lets the SC issue directions, orders or writs, including the five writs?
70.x: 32(2) – SC may issue directions, orders or writs, including the five writs

70.s: Which body may Parliament empower by law under Article 32(3) to exercise the SC's writ powers locally?
70.x: 32(3) – Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise these powers within its local limits – no such law made yet

70.s: Under which Article can the right under Article 32 be suspended?
70.x: 32(4) – The right shall not be suspended except as the Constitution provides (Art. 359)

70.s: Which rights alone does Article 32 enforce?
70.x: What Art. 32 enforces – Only Fundamental Rights – not constitutional, statutory or other rights

70.s: When can the Supreme Court refuse relief under Article 32?
o: When no Fundamental Right is infringed
70.x: Refusal of relief – The SC can refuse relief if no Fundamental Right has been infringed

70.s: Which Amendment ended the right to property as a Fundamental Right?
70.x: Right to property – No longer an FR (44th Amendment, 1978; now Art. 300A) – its violation is challenged under Art. 226 or by a civil suit, not by a writ under Art. 32

70.s: Under which Article does the SC alone hear Centre-State and inter-State disputes?
70.x: Shared jurisdiction – SC and HCs share enforcement of Fundamental Rights; Centre-State and inter-State disputes = SC only (Art. 131)

70.s: Under which Article can the President suspend the right to move courts for named FRs in an Emergency?
70.x: Who suspends FRs – The President – under Art. 359, during a National Emergency, by an order suspending the right to move courts for named FRs

70.s: Which Article suspends Article 19 automatically during an Emergency on grounds of war or external aggression?
70.x: Art. 358 – Suspends Art. 19 automatically (war/external aggression)

70.s: Which Amendment made Arts. 20 and 21 non-suspendable, undoing ADM Jabalpur?
70.x: Arts. 20 and 21 – Cannot be suspended – added by the 44th Amendment (1978) to undo ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), which had upheld suspension of habeas corpus/Art. 21 in the Emergency

70.s: Who imposes limits on Fundamental Rights by law, while the Judiciary only judges their reasonableness?
70.x: Limits on FRs – Imposed by Parliament by law; the Judiciary only judges their reasonableness

70.s: Which Article lets Parliament restrict the FRs of the armed forces and police forces?
70.x: Art. 33 – Parliament (not State legislatures) may restrict or abrogate FRs of the armed forces, paramilitary/forces for public order (police), intelligence or counter-intelligence bodies and persons in telecommunication systems set up for those forces

70.s: What may Parliament do under Article 34 for acts done while martial law is in force?
70.x: Art. 34 – Restrictions while martial law is in force; Parliament may indemnify acts done under it; martial law is not defined in the Constitution

70.s: Who alone legislates under Article 35 to punish offences under Part III?
70.x: Art. 35 – Parliament alone legislates on matters under Arts. 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 and prescribes punishment for Part III offences – a State legislature cannot

70.s: What is the status of Public Interest Litigation, which no Article mentions?
o: No, it is not an FR
70.x: Basis – No Article mentions PIL – a judge-made tool (borrowed from the USA), filed under Arts. 32 and 226; PIL is not itself an FR

70.s: Who may move the court in a PIL for those unable to, under relaxed locus standi?
70.x: Locus standi relaxed – Not only the aggrieved: any public-spirited person may move the court for those unable to – giving the poor and weak access to justice, essential for the rule of law

70.s: Which case saw a prisoner's letter treated as a writ petition (epistolary jurisdiction)?
70.x: Epistolary jurisdiction – Letters/postcards treated as writ petitions – Sunil Batra (prisoner's letter)

70.s: Which 1981 case is a key PIL case linked to Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer?
70.x: S.P. Gupta (1981) – Key PIL case; Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer

71.s: Which 1985 case upheld a divorced Muslim wife's maintenance under Sec. 125 CrPC?
71.x: Shah Bano (1985) – Divorced Muslim wife's maintenance under Sec. 125 CrPC (now 144 BNSS); called for a UCC

71.s: Which 1995 case on conversion for a second marriage is the landmark Uniform Civil Code judgment?
71.x: Sarla Mudgal (1995) – Conversion to contract a second marriage (bigamy); urged a Uniform Civil Code – the landmark UCC judgment

71.s: Which 2000 case followed Sarla Mudgal on conversion and bigamy?
71.x: Lily Thomas (2000) – Followed Sarla Mudgal on conversion and bigamy

71.s: Which 2003 case held that polygamy is not an essential religious practice?
71.x: Javed (2003) – Polygamy not an essential religious practice

71.s: Which 2014 case recognised transgender persons as the third gender?
71.x: NALSA (2014) – Transgender persons = third gender

71.s: What was the majority by which the SC held instant triple talaq void in Shayara Bano (2017)?
71.x: Shayara Bano (2017) – Instant triple talaq void, 3:2; not an essential practice → Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 (up to 3 years) – Parliament endorsed the 2017 ruling

71.s: How many judges read down Section 377 IPC in Navtej Singh Johar (2018)?
71.x: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) – Section 377 IPC read down (consensual adults); five judges, CJI Dipak Misra; it is a Section, not an Article; first read down by the Delhi HC in Naz Foundation (2009)

71.s: Which 2018 case struck down Section 497 IPC on adultery?
71.x: Joseph Shine (2018) – Sec. 497 IPC (adultery) struck down

71.s: Which case: No FR to marry; same-sex marriage left to Parliament?
71.x: Supriyo (Oct 2023) – No FR to marry; same-sex marriage left to Parliament

71.s: Which new criminal code, in force from 1 July 2024, has no adultery offence and no Sec. 377 equivalent?
71.x: BNS (1 July 2024) has no adultery offence and no Sec. 377 equivalent.

71.s: Which 1997 case laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace, later the POSH Act?
71.x: Workplace sexual harassment (Arts. 14, 19(1)(g), 21 – equality and life) → POSH Act 2013 – Vishaka (1997), three judges, CJI J.S. Verma

71.s: Which 2006 case made registration of all marriages compulsory?
71.x: Compulsory registration of all marriages – Seema v. Ashwini Kumar (2006)

71.s: Which 2016 case led to drought management guidelines to the Government of India?
71.x: Drought management guidelines to the Government of India – Swaraj Abhiyan v. Union of India (May 2016)

71.s: What did the SC make the playing of the National Anthem in cinema halls in January 2018?
71.x: National Anthem in cinema halls before films – Supreme Court (Shyam Narayan Chouksey, Nov 2016; made optional in Jan 2018)

71.s: Which 1997 case laid down the arrest memo guidelines?
71.x: Arrest memo – D.K. Basu (1997)

71.s: Which 1980 case allowed handcuffing only in exceptional cases?
71.x: Handcuffing only in exceptional cases – Prem Shankar Shukla (1980)

71.s: Which 2013 case made the FIR mandatory for cognizable offences?
71.x: FIR mandatory for cognizable offences (now 173 BNSS) – Lalita Kumari (2013)

71.s: Which 2006 case gave directions on police reforms?
71.x: Police reforms – Prakash Singh (2006)

71.s: Under which Articles can the SC fill legislative gaps by guidelines until Parliament acts?
71.x: Arts. 32, 141, 142 let the Court fill legislative gaps temporarily until Parliament acts.

71.s: Which 1950 case read Article 21 narrowly, checking only that the procedure in law was followed?
71.x: A.K. Gopalan (1950) – Narrow Art. 21 – the court only checks that the procedure in the law was followed (preventive detention)

71.s: Which 1951 case on a communal G.O. led to the 1st Amendment and Article 15(4)?
71.x: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) – FRs over DPSPs (communal G.O.) → 1st Amendment, Art. 15(4)

71.s: Which case: Advisory: ceding territory needs a constitutional amendment; Preamble not part of the Constitution (reversed in…?
71.x: Berubari (1960) – Advisory: ceding territory needs a constitutional amendment; Preamble not part of the Constitution (reversed in Kesavananda)

71.s: Which 1967 case held that Fundamental Rights cannot be amended?
71.x: Golaknath (1967) – FRs cannot be amended – they let a man "chalk out his life"

71.s: Which 1976 case held FRs including Article 21 unenforceable during the Emergency?
71.x: ADM Jabalpur (1976) – FRs including Art. 21 unenforceable during the Emergency; overruled in Puttaswamy

71.s: Which 1978 case on travel abroad held that procedure must be just, fair and reasonable?
71.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) – Travel abroad; procedure must be just, fair and reasonable; golden triangle 14, 19, 21; life with dignity

71.s: Which 1980 case limited the death penalty to the "rarest of rare" cases?
71.x: Bachan Singh (1980) – Death penalty only in the "rarest of rare" cases

71.s: Which 1982 case read equal pay for equal work from Arts. 14, 16 and 39(d)?
71.x: Randhir Singh (1982) – Equal pay for equal work read from Arts. 14 and 16 with 39(d) and the word "Socialist" in the Preamble

71.s: Which 2015 case struck down Section 66A of the IT Act under Article 19(1)(a)?
71.x: Shreya Singhal (2015) – Sec. 66A IT Act struck down – Art. 19(1)(a)

71.s: Which right did nine judges declare a Fundamental Right in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)?
71.x: K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) – Privacy an FR under Art. 21 / Part III; nine judges, CJI J.S. Khehar; applied to DNA paternity tests

71.s: Which is the correct chronology of these Fundamental Rights cases?
71.x: Chronology of FR cases: Gopalan (1950) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980).

71.s: How many judges decided S.R. Bommai (1994), which made Art. 356 proclamations judicially reviewable?
71.x: S.R. Bommai (1994) – Nine judges; redefined Centre–State relations – Art. 356 proclamations are judicially reviewable; majority to be tested on the floor of the House; secularism and federalism basic

71.s: What did the SC order in Kalyan Singh v. Jagdambika Pal (1998, U.P.)?
71.x: Kalyan Singh v. Jagdambika Pal (February 1998, U.P.) – Composite floor test ordered by the Supreme Court – a single vote between the two rival claimants (Kalyan Singh won 225–196)

71.s: Which 2006 case held the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly void?
71.x: Rameshwar Prasad (2006) – Dissolution of the Bihar Assembly void

71.s: Which 2016 case on Arunachal Pradesh held that the Governor acts on the advice of ministers?
71.x: Nabam Rebia (2016) – Governor acts on advice

71.s: Which April 2025 case held that long-pending Bills had deemed assent?
o: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor
71.x: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (April 2025) – Deemed assent for long-pending Bills

71.s: What did the Presidential reference opinion of November 2025 hold on Governors and Bills?
o: No fixed timelines and no deemed assent
71.x: Presidential reference opinion (November 2025) – No fixed timelines and no deemed assent

71.s: Which 2005 case struck down the IMDT Act for breaching the Union's duty under Art. 355?
71.x: Sarbananda Sonowal (2005) – IMDT Act struck down for breaching the Union's duty under Art. 355

71.s: Which OBC quota did Indra Sawhney (1992) uphold?
71.x: Indra Sawhney (1992) – Upheld the 27% OBC quota; caste can be a factor in identifying backwardness; creamy layer excluded; 50% ceiling; no reservation in promotions (→ 77th Amendment)

71.s: Which 2006 case held that a promotion quota needs quantifiable data on backwardness and efficiency?
71.x: M. Nagaraj (2006) – Promotion quota needs quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequacy and efficiency (Art. 335)

71.s: Which 2024 case let States sub-classify SCs, overruling E.V. Chinnaiah?
o: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
71.x: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (1 Aug 2024) – Seven judges, 6:1; States may sub-classify SCs; overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) (AP Act, 2000)

71.s: Which 2020 case struck down a 100% ST teacher quota in AP Scheduled Areas?
71.x: Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020) – 100% ST teacher quota in AP Scheduled Areas struck down

71.s: Which 2002 case made candidates disclose criminal record, assets and educational qualifications?
71.x: Union of India v. ADR (2002) – Candidates disclose criminal record, assets, educational qualifications

71.s: Which option for voters came from the PUCL (2013) judgment?
71.x: PUCL (2013) – NOTA

71.s: Which provision was struck down in Lily Thomas (2013)?
71.x: Lily Thomas (2013) – Sec. 8(4) RPA struck down

71.s: What did the SC call the CBI in the coal allocation case (2013)?
71.x: Coal allocation case (2013) – CBI a "caged parrot"

71.s: Which 2023 case put Election Commissioners' selection with the PM, LoP and CJI until Parliament made a law?
71.x: Anoop Baranwal (2023) – EC selection by PM, LoP, CJI till Parliament made a law

71.s: Which case: Scheme struck down, unanimous – voters' right to information, Art. 19(1)(a)?
71.x: Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024) – Scheme struck down, unanimous – voters' right to information, Art. 19(1)(a)

71.s: Which case: Panel headed by Justice F.M.I. Kalifulla, with Sri Sri Ravi Shankar and Sriram Panchu as members; the Court…?
71.x: Ayodhya mediation (March 2019) – Panel headed by Justice F.M.I. Kalifulla, with Sri Sri Ravi Shankar and Sriram Panchu as members; the Court decided the case in Nov 2019

71.s: By which date did the Article 370 judgment (11 Dec 2023) order elections in J&K?
71.x: Article 370 (11 Dec 2023) – Five judges under CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, unanimous; Art. 370 a temporary provision; elections by 30 September 2024

71.s: Which case: Upheld 4:1 under Sec. 26(2) RBI Act?
71.x: Demonetisation (Jan 2023) – Upheld 4:1 under Sec. 26(2) RBI Act

71.s: Which case: Bail is the rule even under the UAPA?
71.x: Andrabi v. NIA (May 2026) – Bail is the rule even under the UAPA

71.s: Which landmark judgment came under CJI J.S. Khehar?
71.x: Khehar – Puttaswamy

71.s: Which judgments came under CJI Dipak Misra?
71.x: Dipak Misra – Shayara Bano, Navtej, Aadhaar

71.s: Which judgments came under CJI D.Y. Chandrachud?
71.x: Chandrachud – Art. 370, Electoral Bonds

71.s: From which date is Amaravati the sole capital of Andhra Pradesh?
71.x: Amaravati is the sole capital of AP from 2 June 2024; the AP High Court ruled against the three-capitals plan in 2022.

71.s: Which Amendment had a clause struck down in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)?
71.x: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) – 39th Amendment clause (Art. 329A(4)) struck down; free and fair elections basic; the 44th later undid the 39th's changes

71.s: Which 1980 case held FRs and DPSPs complementary, striking down parts of the 42nd Amendment?
71.x: Minerva Mills (1980) – Linked to the 42nd Amendment; FRs and DPSPs complementary

71.s: Which 1987 case struck down the 32nd Amendment provision Art. 371D(5) for AP?
71.x: P. Sambamurthy (1987) – 32nd Amendment (AP, Art. 371D(5)) struck down

71.s: Which Schedule did Kihoto Hollohan (1992) uphold?
71.x: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) – Upheld the Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment); Speaker's decision reviewable

71.s: What was the majority by which the SC upheld Aadhaar in 2018?
71.x: Verdict – Upheld 4:1

71.s: How long at most may Aadhaar authentication records be kept, as per the 2018 judgment?
71.x: Authentication records – Kept at most 6 months

71.s: Which section of the Aadhaar Act, on use by private entities, was struck down in 2018?
71.x: Sec. 57 (private entities) – Struck down

71.s: For what did the Aadhaar judgment (2018) keep Aadhaar mandatory?
71.x: Mandatory for – Benefits from the Consolidated Fund; PAN/ITR

71.s: For which of these is Aadhaar not mandatory after the 2018 judgment?
71.x: Not mandatory for – Bank accounts, SIM cards, school admissions

71.s: What is Aadhaar not proof of, under Sec. 9 of the Aadhaar Act?
71.x: Sec. 9 – Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship, domicile or date of birth

71.s: Which 1987 case laid down the doctrine of absolute liability?
71.x: Absolute liability – Oleum gas (1987)

71.s: Which 1996 case adopted the precautionary principle and polluter pays?
71.x: Precautionary principle, polluter pays – Vellore Citizens (1996)

71.s: Which 1997 case applied the public trust doctrine?
71.x: Public trust – Kamal Nath (1997)

71.s: Which 1955 case laid down the doctrine of eclipse?
71.x: Eclipse – Bhikaji Narain (1955)

71.s: Which 1953 case dealt with the doctrine of colourable legislation?
71.x: Colourable legislation – Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953)

71.s: In which case did the SC apply the doctrine of prospective overruling?
71.x: Prospective overruling – Golaknath

71.s: Which 1996 case is known as the forest case?
71.x: Forest case – T.N. Godavarman (1996)

72.s: Which UDHR Article parallels Article 14 (equality before law) of the Indian Constitution?
72.x: 14 – Equality before law and equal protection of laws – "State shall not deny to any person" – Art. 7

72.s: Which Article abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form?
72.x: 17 – Untouchability abolished, its practice in any form forbidden; enforcement of any disability an offence

72.s: Who can claim the six freedoms of Article 19?
72.x: 19 – Six freedoms (speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession); citizens only – Arts. 13, 19, 20, 23

72.s: Which Article protects life and personal liberty?
72.x: 21 – Life and personal liberty – Art. 3

72.s: Which UDHR Article parallels Article 21 (life and personal liberty)?
72.x: 21 – Life and personal liberty – Art. 3

72.s: Which Amendment made education for children of 6-14 years a Fundamental Right?
72.x: 21A – Education, 6-14 years (86th Amendment, 2002) – both a human right and a Fundamental Right – Art. 26

72.s: Which UDHR Article parallels Article 21A (right to education)?
72.x: 21A – Education, 6-14 years (86th Amendment, 2002) – both a human right and a Fundamental Right – Art. 26

72.s: Which UDHR Article parallels Article 23 (ban on traffic in human beings and forced labour)?
72.x: 23 – Traffic in human beings, begar and other forced labour prohibited → Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 – Art. 4

72.s: What is the age below which Article 24 bars children from factories, mines and hazardous work?
72.x: 24 – No child below 14 in factories, mines, hazardous work – Arts. 4, 25(2)

72.s: Which UDHR Articles parallel Article 24 (ban on child labour)?
72.x: 24 – No child below 14 in factories, mines, hazardous work – Arts. 4, 25(2)
